bio.en: Bangaly Kaba was an early growth PM at Facebook, Head of Growth at Instagram (scaling it past 1 billion users), VP of Product at Instacart, and is Director of Product Management at YouTube, known for his framework on driving organizational change.
bio.zh: Bangaly Kaba 曾是 Facebook 早期增长产品经理、Instagram 增长负责人（将其扩展到超 10 亿用户）、Instacart 产品副总裁，现任 YouTube 产品管理总监，以其推动组织变革的框架闻名。

summary.en: Bangaly shares a five-component change framework—vision, skills, incentives, resources, action plan—and the discipline of truly understanding a problem before justifying and executing on it. He discusses his legendary “How to Choose Where to Work” essay and how impact depends on the environment and your skills. The conversation is packed with lessons on growth, culture, and making real change inside large organizations.
summary.zh: Bangaly 分享了一个五要素变革框架——愿景、技能、激励、资源、行动计划——以及“先真正理解问题，再论证和执行”的纪律。他谈到了那篇传奇的《如何选择工作与方向》文章，以及影响力如何取决于环境与个人技能。对话充满了关于增长、文化和在大型组织内产生真正变革的洞见。

turns.zh: 是的，我的意思是，所以影响可能有很多方面，但我认为对于产品经理来说，它确实是一个，有助于非常清楚地了解产品的问题在哪里，哪里有机会以及什么是正确的焦点和优先级？这实际上是一种影响。只是创造人们需要理解和相信投资的清晰度。我之所以这样命名，感觉有点违反直觉，是因为你的级别越高，就越会质疑我们是否投资在正确的地方，对吗？这个领域、这个团队、这个组织是正确的投资吗？因此，能够明确表明存在机会，这是正确的事情，在战略和结构上都很重要，是一种影响形式。然后实际实现这种影响，表明你可以快速取得进展，你可以像凯西温特斯所说的那样实现快车道胜利，或者中等和缓慢的胜利，然后实际表明你可以一次又一次地做到这一点，这就是你如何真正验证影响，你可以看到机会在哪里以及正在发生的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. So this equation is impact equals environment type skills. Can you talk a bit about how to work on these two elements?
turns.zh: 惊人的。好的。所以这个等式是影响等于环境类型技能。您能谈谈如何处理这两个要素吗？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: So the environment was the one to me, that I think is most people overlook and I overlooked when I was first thinking about this. Environment in this case, I think I kind of discreetly named a few things. One is your manager, then there's the resources. So what kind of team do you have? Is your team staffed appropriately? Do you have the right P&L, whatever budget to get the things done that you need? Then there's a scope, what is in your remit versus not in your remit? Because if you don't have enough scope, then you can't actually focus on the things that are most important. The team itself, the skills, relative skills of the team, your compensation in some ways is part of the environment because if you're not compensated fairly, you don't believe you are, then it's hard to feel like the work that you're doing is meaningful. (00:11:47): And then there is the last part is the company culture. So to what extent is the culture a place where you feel supported, included, you feel like you can do your best work? And so you are really looking at each one of these variables, and I look at this every year and I say, "How is my manager doing?" How do I think about my manager? How do I think about the resources I have, the scope, the team, the conversation, the company culture and to what extent? And I score them, I score them as a 1 means it's kind of neutral. A 2 means that I'm greatly benefiting from this situation and something even closer to zero is I'm not in a good place. So I assign a score in quarter point increments, 0.25, 0.5, 0.751 up to 2 every year. And I really ask myself, what is the state of each one of these and to what extent do I believe that they can and will change?
turns.zh: 所以环境对我来说是一个，我认为大多数人都忽视了这一点，而当我第一次考虑这个问题时我也忽视了这一点。在这种情况下，我想我谨慎地命名了一些东西。一是你的经理，二是资源。那么你们有什么样的团队呢？您的团队配备合适吗？无论预算如何，您是否有正确的损益表来完成您需要的事情？然后还有一个范围，什么是在你的职权范围内，什么是不在你的职权范围内？因为如果你没有足够的范围，那么你实际上就无法专注于最重要的事情。团队本身、团队的技能、相关技能、你的报酬在某些方面都是环境的一部分，因为如果你没有得到公平的报酬，你不相信自己是公平的，那么你就很难觉得你所做的工作是有意义的。 (00:11:47)：最后一部分是公司文化。那么，这种文化在多大程度上是让你感到支持、包容、让你觉得自己能做到最好的工作的地方呢？所以你真的会关注这些变量中的每一个，我每年都会关注这个变量，然后我会说：“我的经理做得怎么样？”我如何看待我的经理？我如何考虑我拥有的资源、范围、团队、对话、公司文化以及程度如何？我给他们打分，我给他们打分 1 意味着它是中性的。 2 意味着我从这种情况中受益匪浅，更接近于零的是我处境不佳。因此，我每年都会以四分之一分的增量分配分数，从 0.25、0.5、0.751 一直到 2。我真的问自己，其中每一个的状态是什么？我相信它们能够并且将会改变到什么程度？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, I love this. So there's this formula, impact equals environment times skills. Within environment there's these five variables and they add up to 10?
turns.zh: 哇，我喜欢这个。所以有这个公式，影响力等于环境乘以技能。环境中有这五个变量，它们加起来是 10？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If they each give you two points. That's so cool. Okay, so the five, just to be clear, your manager, the resources you have, is teams number three?
turns.zh: 如果他们每人给你两分。太酷了。好的，所以，要明确的是，五个团队，你的经理，你拥有的资源，是第三个团队吗？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯嗯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Compensation and then the culture of the team?
turns.zh: 薪酬，然后是团队文化？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: And then your scope as well.
turns.zh: 然后还有你的范围。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then scope. Okay, got it.
turns.zh: 然后是范围。好的，明白了。

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: It's actually six, yeah.
turns.zh: 实际上是六，是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, there's six. Okay, got it. So it's up to 12. So the idea here is you score each of these of how you're feeling, how the environment is contributing to the impact that you're delivering. And if one of these is not a great score, that's an opportunity to improve your impact, which will improve your career?
turns.zh: 哦，有六个。好的，明白了。因此，最多为 12。因此，这里的想法是，您对自己的感受以及环境如何对您所产生的影响做出贡献的每一项进行评分。如果其中一项得分不是很高，那么这是一个提高你的影响力的机会，这会改善你的职业生涯吗？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: That's right, and you have to really be honest. I think part of what makes this framework so powerful for me at least, is that it helps you to be honest around what are the things that are limiting your ability to have impact and for your skills to really land? And to what extent do you believe that you can help to change or try to influence the change in the environment? Because no one wants to be in a place where there's a bad culture and the culture is a bad fit for you, but if you're not really thinking about it objectively and naming that, or maybe it's the culture of the team that is not the right place for you, so it really forces you to evaluate what's going on around you that's limiting your impact.
turns.zh: 没错，而且你必须非常诚实。我认为这个框架至少对我来说如此强大的部分原因是，它可以帮助你诚实地认识到哪些因素限制了你发挥影响力以及限制你的技能真正发挥作用的能力？您认为您可以在多大程度上帮助改变或尝试影响环境的变化？因为没有人愿意去一个文化不好的地方，而且这种文化不适合你，但如果你没有真正客观地思考并指出它，或者团队的文化不适合你，那么它真的会迫使你评估周围发生的事情，从而限制了你的影响力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example from your career you could share where one of these was not where it needed to be and either helped change it or realize you had to get out of there?
turns.zh: 在你的职业生涯中，有没有一个可以分享的例子，其中一个没有达到它需要的位置，要么帮助改变它，要么意识到你必须离开那里？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: When I was actually at Facebook, I was running the team that does all the people recommendations and it was a great team. I actually had a massive, massive team. I had 30 engineers I was working with, 15 machine learning engineers and 15 front end and back end engineers. And so great team, incredible team, lot of resources, ton of scope. In some ways it was too much scope and to me that was problematic because I really needed to build out, I felt like multiple teams to support the work that we were doing or to break it up; because it was, I mean the pace, the velocity you can imagine at Facebook was incredible. And I felt like between all of the work that we needed to do, the amount of engineering capacity that we had and the amount that was on the table, I felt like I wasn't resourced in a way where I felt like I could actually deliver on all of the things that were necessary without burning myself out. And I felt like I was burning myself out and I couldn't really see the forest through the trees because there was so much to do. (00:15:20): And so that was a situation that I didn't really understand how to navigate at that point in my career. And there were two or three manager changes concurrently, and so I didn't have a manager to lean on that I felt like I had a relationship with to help me to navigate that space. And I felt like the scope was actually too much for what needed to be done, and so I needed to find a better kind of fit for me. There was nothing wrong with the team, it was a great learning environment, but it was the confluence of scope and manager and all happening at once just wasn't a good fit for me.
turns.zh: 当我实际上在 Facebook 时，我负责管理一个负责所有人员推荐的团队，这是一个很棒的团队。我实际上有一个非常非常庞大的团队。与我共事的工程师有 30 名，其中有 15 名机器学习工程师以及 15 名前端和后端工程师。如此伟大的团队，令人难以置信的团队，大量的资源，大量的范围。在某些方面，范围太大，对我来说这是有问题的，因为我确实需要扩展，我觉得需要多个团队来支持我们正在做的工作或将其分解；因为，我的意思是，你可以想象 Facebook 的速度和速度是令人难以置信的。我觉得在我们需要做的所有工作、我们拥有的工程能力和摆在桌面上的工作量之间，我觉得我没有足够的资源，让我觉得我可以在不让自己精疲力尽的情况下真正交付所有必要的事情。我感觉自己快要精疲力尽了，而且我无法真正透过树木看到森林，因为有太多事情要做。 (00:15:20)：所以在我职业生涯的那个阶段，我并不真正了解如何应对这种情况。同时有两三个经理发生变化，所以我没有一个可以依靠的经理，我觉得我与他有关系来帮助我驾驭这个空间。我觉得范围实际上对于需要做的事情来说太多了，所以我需要找到一种更适合我的方式。团队没有任何问题，这是一个很好的学习环境，但它是范围和经理的融合，所有事情同时发生并不适合我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A lot of people are in these situations where they'd say they go through this score, they identify I have way too little scope, way too much scope like you described, and there's always this question of can I actually make a change or is this just not, am I not in a position? Especially, I see product managers, there's just always a lot of, I can't actually change anything. What do you often tell people around this that just feel like there's nothing I can do here and my manager sucks, what am I going to do?
turns.zh: 很多人都处于这种情况下，他们会说他们经历了这个分数，他们发现我的范围太小，就像你所描述的那样，范围太大，并且总是存在这样的问题：我是否可以真正做出改变，或者这只是不能，我是否不适合？特别是，我看到产品经理，总是有很多，我实际上无法改变任何东西。你经常告诉周围的人，感觉我在这里无能为力，而且我的经理很糟糕，我该怎么办？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: Well, I do think one of the things that I recognize is your manager. Not all of these variables is created equal and the manager is the most important variable in the environment, because a great manager who is empathetic, who is aware of what's going on, who is a great communicator, has the ability to move the chess pieces around and to fix some of these for you either immediately or in time. There's no one other than your manager who can really help to increase your scope or to help make sure that the team has the right pieces in place, or dial in some of the issues that you might see in culture. (00:16:56): And so that is why people say they don't leave a job, they leave a manager because the manager is the one that has a lot of the power to fix a lot of these variables. And so really the question becomes like to what extent have you been able to clearly articulate what are the... And dispassionately articulate, what are the challenges that you're having, you're seeing across some of these variables with your manager? Help them to tie it back to how it's impacting your work and see if they can help you to create a plan to alleviate some of these things.
turns.zh: 嗯，我确实认为我认识的人之一就是你的经理。并非所有这些变量都是平等的，经理是环境中最重要的变量，因为一位优秀的经理具有同理心，了解正在发生的事情，是一位出色的沟通者，有能力移动棋子并立即或及时为您解决其中的一些问题。除了您的经理之外，没有人可以真正帮助您扩大范围或帮助确保团队拥有正确的部分，或者解决您可能在文化中遇到的一些问题。 (00:16:56)：这就是为什么人们说他们离开的不是工作，而是经理，因为经理拥有很大的权力来解决很多这些变量。因此，真正的问题是，您在多大程度上能够清楚地阐明……并且冷静地阐明，您所面临的挑战是什么，您与经理一起看到了其中的一些变量？帮助他们将其与它对您工作的影响联系起来，看看他们是否可以帮助您制定一个计划来缓解其中的一些问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's super interesting. Then your experience with the manager is kind of the core of a lot of these variables. Is there anything you recommend to people if their managers is not someone they like, is it just try to find a new manager or potentially leave?
turns.zh: 这太有趣了。那么你与经理的经历就是许多这些变量的核心。如果人们的经理不是他们喜欢的人，您有什么建议吗？是尝试寻找新经理还是可能离开？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: You're never going to always like your manager, right? That's not the... The goal isn't to like your manager. Ideally, you respect them and they respect you, you feel like there's things that you can learn from them. Finding a new manager is always an option, but I guess sometimes the real question is, is actually spending time to try to understand what is your manager optimizing? A lot of times I think there is a big disconnect between an IC focusing on their discrete area and try to optimize for local maxima, versus understanding, okay, my manager's thinking about these things and this is how I fit in, and understanding maybe they have a gap to understanding why your area is important. Or maybe there's stuff that's on your manager's plate that is actually adjacent to your remit that if you understood that they were optimizing for, you can take that on and you would find more synergies with what they're trying to do.
turns.zh: 你永远不会永远喜欢你的经理，对吗？那不是……目标不是喜欢你的经理。理想情况下，你尊重他们，他们也尊重你，你觉得你可以从他们身上学到一些东西。寻找新经理始终是一种选择，但我想有时真正的问题是，是否真的花时间尝试了解您的经理正在优化什么？很多时候，我认为 IC 专注于其离散区域并尝试优化局部最大值与理解（好吧，我的经理正在考虑这些事情，这就是我的适应方式）之间存在很大的脱节，而理解也许他们与理解为什么你的区域很重要之间存在很大的差距。或者，也许你的经理的职责范围内有一些事情实际上与你的职权范围相邻，如果你了解他们正在优化的目标，你就可以承担这个任务，你会发现与他们正在尝试做的事情有更多的协同作用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that advice. Let's talk about the other side of this equation. We've talked about environment, let's talk about skills. What do you advise there for folks that want to improve their skills?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个建议。让我们谈谈这个等式的另一边。谈完了环境，我们再来谈谈技能。对于那些想要提高技能的人，您有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: The skills part is really, really big and it's something that requires I think, consistent evolution of your own abilities. And so I broke it out in that blog post kind of communication, your ability to influence your leadership, strategic thinking and then execution, actually getting things done. The communication above these, again, not all of these are created equal. I think communication is the one that tends to be the most impactful. And you see this in a lot of ways. You see this for people who are poor executors but incredible communicators and they seem to continue to rise and rise because they can tell a great story, but when you look under the covers, there's nothing there. There's no substance there. (00:19:17): So communication for better or worse is one of the most important things. But building out your skills I think is really just kind of a, it is an interesting time to be in product and to be in tech right now because you have so many more ways to build out your skills than what previously existed. Just so many incredible blog posts like your podcasts and blogs, there's so many incredible people who've come on here who tell you things like how to go to market, how to think about B2B SaaS and metrics. And so listening to you, reading Ben Thompson, understanding his mental models, if you go to look at Elena Verner or whoever, there's so many thought leaders who are out there. (00:19:56): So I think being a voracious reader is really, really critical because it helps to build your toolkit and you need arrows in your quiver to really understand how to think about the right framework and the right mentor at the right time. (00:20:09): One thing I also tell people is people think about mentorship as like, I have a mentor, Lenny is my mentor, or John is my mentor. I tell them, it's actually better to have a stable of mentors. You want to have three or four. And ideally, what you do is you meet with each one of them once a month on a different Friday of the month. And so you might have three or four people on every Friday you're meeting with someone different. And the reason why this is so important is because if you, Lenny, are a mentor to me and you're busy one Friday and we only meet once a month now I don't have anyone to talk to for two months. And you're going through a lot of things and you're not really able to bounce ideas, or build skills or learn how influence others, but if you have three or four mentors, you have someone different to talk to every week. And if one or two of them cancel, you still have two people to talk to that month and you still can continue to grow and to build your thinking. (00:21:01): So that's something I always recommend. And then the last thing I actually talk about is, when it comes to execution, I think people don't, especially product managers, don't do enough of watching and learning from others. There's an art and a science to product management. And in a lot of ways I come from a background of education and in a lot of ways in product management, it's very similar. You want to watch how well the people hone their craft, how they deliver, how they lead teams and kind of steal things from them. Figure out, well, wow, Lenny did this really, really well when he was at Airbnb. It was really incredible. I'm going to take that. I'm going to take how he runs that team, or how he landed that framework, or how he communicated this message and note it and use it in my own toolkit later on. And so if you're really a student of product, you can't just be a student of theory, you've got to be a student of practice too, meaning you're going and you're looking, it's like, "Hey, I'd love to sit in your team meetings. Can I come watch? Or your PM meetings or your leadership meetings." And you are really like doing that for the sake of learning is really, really incredible. And that's some of the ways I talk about building skills.
turns.zh: 技能部分真的非常非常大，我认为这需要你自己能力的持续发展。因此，我在那篇博文中阐述了沟通的方式，即影响领导力、战略思维和执行力的能力，以及实际完成工作的能力。再说一遍，以上的沟通并非所有这些都是平等的。我认为沟通往往是最有影响力的一种。你可以从很多方面看到这一点。你可以在那些执行力差但沟通能力强的人身上看到这一点，他们似乎会不断崛起，因为他们可以讲述一个伟大的故事，但当你看到幕后，你会发现里面什么也没有。那里没有任何物质。 (00:19:17)：因此无论好坏，沟通都是最重要的事情之一。但我认为培养你的技能实际上只是一种，现在是产品和技术领域的一个有趣的时刻，因为你有比以前更多的方法来培养你的技能。有这么多令人难以置信的博客文章，比如您的播客和博客，还有这么多令人难以置信的人来到这里，告诉您如何进入市场、如何考虑 B2B SaaS 和指标等事情。因此，听听你的讲话，阅读本·汤普森（Ben Thompson），了解他的思维模式，如果你去看看埃琳娜·维尔纳（Elena Verner）或其他人，就会发现那里有很多思想领袖。 (00:19:56)：所以我认为成为一名贪婪的读者真的非常重要，因为它有助于构建你的工具包，你需要箭袋里的箭头才能真正理解如何在正确的时间思考正确的框架和正确的导师。 (00:20:09)：我还告诉人们的一件事是，人们认为导师制就像是，我有一位导师，莱尼是我的导师，或者约翰是我的导师。我告诉他们，拥有稳定的导师实际上更好。你想要三四个。理想情况下，您所做的就是每月在不同的星期五与他们每个人会面一次。因此，每个星期五您可能会与三四个人会面，与不同的人会面。这之所以如此重要，是因为如果你，莱尼，是我的导师，而你在某个周五很忙，而我们每个月只见一次面，那么现在我已经两个月没有人可以交谈了。你正在经历很多事情，你实际上无法激发想法、培养技能或学习如何影响他人，但如果你有三到四位导师，那么你每周都会有不同的人可以交谈。如果其中一两个人取消，那个月你仍然有两个人可以交谈，你仍然可以继续成长并建立你的想法。 (00:21:01)：所以这是我一直推荐的。然后我真正谈论的最后一件事是，当谈到执行时，我认为人们，尤其是产品经理，没有做足够的观察和向他人学习。产品管理既是一门艺术，也是一门科学。在很多方面，我都有教育背景，在产品管理方面也有很多方面，这非常相似。你想观察人们如何磨练自己的技艺、如何交付、如何领导团队以及如何从他们那里窃取东西。想想看，哇哦，莱尼在 Airbnb 的时候在这方面做得非常非常好。实在是太不可思议了。我要接受这个。我将了解他如何管理该团队，或者他如何实现该框架，或者他如何传达此消息并记下它并稍后在我自己的工具包中使用它。因此，如果你真的是产品的学生，你不能只是理论的学生，你也必须成为实践的学生，这意味着你要去并且你正在寻找，就像，“嘿，我很想参加你的团队会议。我可以来观看吗？或者你的 PM 会议或领导会议。”你真的喜欢为了学习而这样做，这真的非常非常令人难以置信。这就是我谈论培养技能的一些方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of that latter lesson that you learned from someone that comes to mind of watching someone and like, oh, I'm going to do that.
turns.zh: 后一个教训有没有一个例子，你从某人那里学到的，当你想到观察某人时，你会想，哦，我要这么做。

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: Earlier in my career, when I first got to Instagram, I wasn't the first Growth PM, but I was one of the first and a guy who was there before me, his name was Georgia Lee, he actually stood up the growth team and ended up leaving six months right after I joined. But I watched, George was a really good listener. He had just a really incredible ability to be in a room and hear what was going on, to recast it back and make sure that everyone felt good about where we were and what was being said and the path forward, and really crystallizing the action items and also how people felt about what the next steps were. And walking out of that meeting, it felt like he always had buy-in and clarity and was helpful to build trust. You can see him almost winning trust in every moment of that meeting. And that was something that I really admired, and learned, and kind sought to emulate later on in my career.
turns.zh: 在我职业生涯的早期，当我第一次加入 Instagram 时，我不是第一个增长 PM，但我是第一个，而且是在我之前的人之一，他的名字叫 Georgia Lee，他实际上支持了增长团队，并在我加入后六个月就离开了。但我观察到，乔治是一个非常好的倾听者。他有一种非常令人难以置信的能力，能够在一个房间里听到正在发生的事情，将其重新演绎，并确保每个人都对我们所处的位置、所说的内容和前进的道路感到满意，并真正具体化行动项目以及人们对下一步的感受。离开那次会议后，我感觉他总是持支持态度，思路清晰，有助于建立信任。你可以看到他在那次会议的每一刻几乎都赢得了信任。这是我真正钦佩、学到的东西，也是我后来在职业生涯中寻求效仿的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an awesome example. It comes back to the skill of communication that you talked about, just the power becoming really good at that. And this is such a simple skill you just described, is just recapping, here's what we talked about. Here's what we're going to do. Here's the decisions we made. Here's action items. It's not actually difficult, it's just-
turns.zh: 这是一个很棒的例子。这又回到了你谈到的沟通技巧，就是变得非常擅长沟通的能力。这是您刚才描述的一项简单技能，只是回顾一下，这就是我们讨论的内容。这就是我们要做的。这是我们做出的决定。这是行动项目。其实并不难，只是——

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: It's not, actually. But what was magical about the way he did it. It's like he would name people and their contributions and show how all of this came together into what is the path forward.
turns.zh: 事实上并非如此。但他的做法有何神奇之处。就好像他会列出人们的名字和他们的贡献，并展示所有这些如何共同形成前进的道路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is amazing.
turns.zh: 这真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: And it's the communication, but it's also the other side. It's the other coin, the side of communication, which is eliciting to figure out how you communicate back to others.
turns.zh: 这是沟通，但也是另一面。这是另一枚硬币，即沟通的一面，它促使你弄清楚如何与他人沟通。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So good. Following up on something else you talked about, which is mentors. Anytime someone talks about finding mentors, everyone's always, how do I find a mentor? What advice do you share with folks of how to find a mentor to help? You say once a week or once a month?
turns.zh: 超好的。继续你谈到的其他事情，那就是导师。每当有人谈到寻找导师时，大家总是会问，我该如何寻找导师呢？关于如何寻找导师来提供帮助，您有什么建议与大家分享？你说每周一次还是每月一次？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: Where I see people find the most success is they ask. They tell people what they're working on or what challenges they have and they say, "Do you know someone who I might be able to learn from who has done this or has good thinking about this recently?" So instead of just going to someone saying, "Hey, can you be a mentor?" Coming to me and say, "Hey, Bengaly, I'm actually trying to figure out how do I change the way this team operates because we need to go from this model to that model, but here's some of the challenges. So do you know someone who's actually really good at changing the way teams work or really good at communicating a new vision that I can talk to?" (00:24:40): And so that I think is really important because what you do is you're creating a seed, and the seed is there's a triad and you have the person who's looking for the mentor. You have the recommender, the recommender, and then you have the potential mentor. And the recommender is basically saying, "Here, there's common purpose between the two of you and I can see it, and I think this is important, so I want you all to come together." And that triad in that moment creates a higher affinity, highly likelihood that the person who needs the help and the person who you're connecting them with are going to see mutual benefit from one another. And I think I find that just doing that and seeding that and being really focused on what the opportunity or the challenge is, tends to lead to better connections as opposed to just reaching out and saying, "Hey, I like your style. Will you be my mentor?"
turns.zh: 我发现人们最成功的地方就是他们提出要求。他们告诉人们他们正在做什么或面临什么挑战，然后他们说：“你知道有谁做过这件事，或者最近对此有很好的思考，我可以向他学习吗？”因此，不要只是去找某人说：“嘿，你能成为一名导师吗？”来找我说，“嘿，Bengaly，我实际上想弄清楚如何改变这个团队的运作方式，因为我们需要从这个模型转向那个模型，但这里有一些挑战。那么你知道有人真正擅长改变团队工作方式，或者真正擅长传达我可以与之交谈的新愿景吗？” (00:24:40)：所以我认为这非常重要，因为你所做的就是创造一颗种子，而种子就是有一个三合会，并且你有一个正在寻找导师的人。你有推荐人，推荐人，然后你就有潜在的导师。推荐人基本上是在说，“在这里，你们两个之间有共同的目标，我可以看到它，我认为这很重要，所以我希望你们所有人走到一起。”在那一刻，三合会创造了一种更高的亲和力，极有可能需要帮助的人和与你联系的人会看到彼此的共同利益。我认为我发现，仅仅这样做、播种并真正关注机会或挑战是什么，往往会带来更好的联系，而不是仅仅伸出手说：“嘿，我喜欢你的风格。你愿意成为我的导师吗？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So essentially share with folks you trust, here's what I'm working on. See if they recommend someone that could help you with that specific skill versus assuming that there's this person that can help you with this skill?
turns.zh: 因此，基本上与您信任的人分享，这就是我正在做的事情。看看他们是否会推荐可以帮助您掌握该特定技能的人，而不是假设这个人可以帮助您掌握该技能？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 这是正确的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. Going back to your advice on career, something that you wrote about in your post plus folks have told me you're really big on, is this something you call understand work? Does that ring a bell?
turns.zh: 我喜欢它。回到你对职业的建议，你在帖子中写到的东西，加上人们告诉我你真的很喜欢，这是你所谓的理解工作吗？这是否敲响了警钟？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: Yes, it does.
turns.zh: 是的，确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Talk about that and why that's important?
turns.zh: 好的。谈谈这个以及为什么这很重要？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: I certainly cannot take credit for understand work. This is part of an old Facebook framework of understand, identify, execute. What I-
turns.zh: 我当然不能因为理解工作而获得荣誉。这是旧的 Facebook 理解、识别、执行框架的一部分。我什么-

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: Facebook framework of understand, identify, execute. What I probably will say is I guess I've been the shepherd for understand work in other companies. I've taken it from my time at Facebook and Relink Institute or rigorously at Instagram, then at Instacart and when I helped with Twitter, now at YouTube. The way I like to talk about it with my teams is that first I tell a story actually, and the story is we've all had a moment where we have worked on something with a team, super excited, finally it launches and we go out to dinner and we celebrate. And we're celebrating, everyone's juiced. It's great night. You go back to the office the next day and you look at the metrics and the metrics are flat and everyone's a little bummed. Why did this happen? Right. Why are the metrics flat? What happened? We worked so hard. (00:26:49): And ultimately when you unpack it, you realize that you built something that you thought was going to be a good idea, but you really didn't understand a lot of key components of what people really needed, what pain points really existed, or what were the alternatives and what the real value of those alternatives were in the market, or exactly how the product needed to work, what the flywheel or what the experience needed to be. And so that is what I call the anti-pattern of what we want to do and I call that identify, justify, execute. Right. Where you identify something, someone says, "Hey, you know what? This would be great to build." And you identify that, then you go pull data to go justify why that would be great to build and then you sink an ungodly amount of time working on it in order to make it work, but it ultimately doesn't succeed. (00:27:36): And that is the anti-pattern to what is kind of like the Facebook kind of way of thinking, which is understand, identify, execute, right? So first you have to really understand from first principles what is actually going on. So when we talk about understand work, there's a few ways to think about it. One is, it is an intentional affordance in your execution to do the work that helps you to de-risk a project and to learn what's going on. When I say an intentional affordance, meaning you put it down like Lenny is going to work on this thing. Right. Lenny as a product manager is going to write a strategy. Janice as a designer is going to design a prototype, whatever the thing is, and you put it down as actual an item as opposed to assuming it's going to happen in the background. We don't make an affordance for understand work, then the work doesn't get done and everyone's just sprinting on execution. (00:28:27): And so it's a planned intentional time to the team's bandwidth to figure out what is it that we need to do to understand what's happening. And so for example at Instagram we did a lot of understand work of what makes for a good connection? Right. How do we want to think about that? How do we want to make sure that we're actually growing a graph, a social graph that makes sense? And so I might work with data science to do understand work, to pull a funnel and look at the different types of connections for different types of users and make it make sense. Right. And engineering might do understand work to instrument logging to make sure that we have the data that we need in order to tell the story. And so you're doing this understand work to basically better understand the gaps in knowledge. What's also really interesting is that understand work helps you to clarify what is a root cause, or what is a job to be done, or what is the right use case? (00:29:25): And because the team adopts this mentality, it becomes this forcing function for execution. So when someone says, "You know what we should build? We should build this." You have a team that's enabled and empowered to say, "That's a good idea, but we don't actually understand these three things before we start working on that. So maybe we should do understand work to make sure that that is actually the right idea." Right. And so what you end up getting by embracing this concept is two things. You get parallel paths of work. So every sprint, let's say you do a three-week sprint or a three-month roadmap, you're executing on the things that you have a lot of conviction around and you're also doing understand work in parallel. And so at the end of the sprint you have learnings from what you executed. Wow, that test or that launch worked really well. We should double down. Or Wow, that test or launch didn't work. Here's how we should pivot. And you have insights from the understand work and you use both of those to plan the next sprints or roadmap. Right. (00:30:29): And so because you have this parallel path, you end up getting this velocity multiplier over time. Right. So the next sprint, and the third sprint, and the fourth sprint, every subsequent sprint you de-risk new ideas, you've gotten more clarity. And so you do more execution, you do better execution and you move faster and the things you ship, you have a higher win rate on the things you ship, right? And your shipping, I remember when I left Instagram, this is many years ago, but we had 15 teams and we might've been running 12 to 20 experiments a quarter a team, and I would say probably 60 to 70% of them were positive and shippable, which is incredible. I mean, you think about and multiple and the magnitude of that and it was because we were so effective at de-risking and understanding what was going on.
turns.zh: Facebook 的理解、识别、执行框架。我可能会说的是，我想我一直是其他公司理解工作的引导者。我从我在 Facebook 和 Relink Institute 的经历中学到了这一点，或者严格地在 Instagram 上，然后在 Instacart 上，以及在 Twitter 上提供帮助时，现在在 YouTube 上。我喜欢和我的团队谈论这个问题的方式是，首先我实际上讲一个故事，这个故事是我们都有过这样的时刻，我们和一个团队一起工作，非常兴奋，最后它启动了，我们出去吃晚饭，我们庆祝。我们正在庆祝，每个人都兴奋不已。这是一个美好的夜晚。第二天你回到办公室，查看指标​​，发现指标持平，每个人都有点沮丧。为什么会发生这种情况？正确的。为什么指标持平？发生了什么？我们非常努力。 (00:26:49)：最终，当你打开它时，你会意识到你构建了一些你认为是个好主意的东西，但你真的不了解人们真正需要什么、真正存在什么痛点、或者替代方案是什么以及这些替代方案在市场上的真正价值是什么、或者产品到底需要如何工作、飞轮或体验需要什么等很多关键组成部分。这就是我所说的我们想做的事情的反模式，我称之为识别、证明、执行。正确的。当你识别出某些东西时，有人会说：“嘿，你知道吗？这构建起来非常棒。”你确定了这一点，然后你去提取数据来证明为什么构建它会很棒，然后你投入了大量的时间来使其工作，但最终没有成功。 (00:27:36)：这就是 Facebook 思维方式的反模式，即理解、识别、执行，对吧？因此，首先你必须从基本原则真正理解到底发生了什么。因此，当我们谈论理解工作时，有几种思考方式。一是，它是您执行工作时有意提供的功能，可以帮助您降低项目风险并了解正在发生的情况。当我说有意提供时，意思是你把它放下，就像莱尼要处理这件事一样。正确的。莱尼作为产品经理要写一个策略。作为一名设计师，珍妮丝将设计一个原型，无论是什么，你都将其视为实际的项目，而不是假设它会在后台发生。我们不提供理解工作的能力，那么工作就无法完成，每个人都只是冲刺执行。 (00:28:27)：因此，这是一个计划好的团队带宽时间，旨在弄清楚我们需要做什么来了解正在发生的事情。例如，在 Instagram，我们做了很多了解什么才能建立良好联系的工作？正确的。我们要如何思考这个问题？我们如何确保我们实际上正在生成一个图表，一个有意义的社交图表？因此，我可能会与数据科学合作来理解工作，拉出一个漏斗并查看不同类型用户的不同类型的连接并使其有意义。正确的。工程学可能确实了解仪器记录的工作，以确保我们拥有讲述故事所需的数据。所以你做这个理解工作基本上是为了更好地理解知识差距。真正有趣的是，理解工作可以帮助您澄清根本原因是什么，或者要完成的工作是什么，或者正确的用例是什么？ (00:29:25): 因为团队采用了这种心态，所以它就成为执行的强制功能。因此，当有人说：“你知道我们应该构建什么吗？我们应该构建这个。”你有一个团队，他们有能力并有权说：“这是一个好主意，但在我们开始研究之前，我们实际上并不理解这三件事。所以也许我们应该做理解工作，以确保这实际上是正确的想法。”正确的。因此，通过接受这个概念，你最终会得到两件事。你会得到并行的工作路径。因此，每次冲刺，假设您进行了为期三周的冲刺或三个月的路线图，您都在执行您坚信的事情，并且同时也在做理解工作。因此，在冲刺结束时，您可以从执行的内容中学到一些东西。哇，那个测试或那个发布效果非常好。我们应该加倍努力。或者哇，那个测试或发布没有成功。这是我们应该如何转向的。您可以从理解工作中获得见解，并使用这两者来规划下一个冲刺或路线图。正确的。 (00:30:29)：因为你有这条平行路径，所以随着时间的推移，你最终会得到这个速度倍增。正确的。因此，在下一个冲刺、第三个冲刺和第四个冲刺中，每个后续冲刺都会降低新想法的风险，你会变得更加清晰。所以你会执行更多，执行得更好，行动更快，你所交付的东西，你所交付的东西的获胜率会更高，对吗？至于你的发货，我记得当我离开 Instagram 时，这是很多年前的事了，但我们有 15 个团队，每个团队可能会进行 12 到 20 个实验，我想说其中可能有 60 到 70% 是积极的并且可以发货，这是令人难以置信的。我的意思是，你会仔细考虑其重要性，这是因为我们在降低风险和了解正在发生的事情方面非常有效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is really interesting. I imagine many people listening here are like, we put time into understanding, we run experiments, we write strategy docs, we use research. What is it that you think people are, where do you think they're missing? Is it that you dedicate people's actual time, like you're just doing understand work instead of building a new thing. For this next sprint, you're just going to be telling us what the problem here or opportunity is. How do you actually operationalize this versus just what people probably already do, which is user research, data dives?
turns.zh: 这真的很有趣。我想很多在这里听的人都会说，我们投入时间来理解，我们进行实验，我们编写策略文档，我们进行研究。你认为人是什么？你认为他们在哪里失踪？是不是你投入了人们的实际时间，就像你只是在做理解工作而不是构建一个新事物一样。对于下一个冲刺，您只需告诉我们这里的问题或机会是什么。与人们可能已经做的事情（用户研究、数据潜水）相比，你如何实际实施这一点？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: What I found is a couple things. One is when your team does not fully understand a problem space, the balance of work tends to be higher. I think when I started at YouTube we were doing 60% execution, 40% understand work. Right. And over time, as we understand more and more, the mix shifts. Now my teams are probably doing 80% execution, 20 to or 85% and 20 to 15% understand work. (00:32:18): And so it's not just about writing a strategy, it's about saying, okay, if we have these themes of stuff that we want to work on, what do we know with confidence because the data tells us and what do we need to understand because we don't have the data, we don't have the research, we don't have the insights? And really being honest with yourselves around what are the things that are low to medium effort but high likelihood of being impactful because you have the data and what are the things that you are interested in perhaps doing, but because you're missing something, you're missing research or feedback from users or data or some insights or strategy. You should actually say, I'm going to go do this before I do something else. Right. (00:33:03): An example of this is one of my teams ships paid virtual goods in the live experience on YouTube. And that's a really, really important and hard problem space. And when I joined, we didn't really fully understand the whole live ecosystem, like how we lived in that live ecosystem, how our products worked, where the biggest opportunity was. So the first and most important piece of understand work was instead of shipping iterations to the current product, we needed to actually get the funnel of what was happening. Right. Like what's happening with how many people are watching live every day, how many people are clicking through, how many people are seeing our experience, how many people actually buying it? We didn't really fully have the experience mapped out and to understand where were the gaps and where are the problem space is in, where should we be focusing? (00:33:52): And so we had to do that. And that was understand work for multiple people, for multiple teams. We had to do on the engineering side, we needed data science as analysis. We needed the PM to go and dog through the experience to figure out what was broken. All of that was intentional and an affordance on our roadmaps.
turns.zh: 我发现有几件事。一是当你的团队没有完全理解某个问题空间时，工作的平衡性往往会更高。我想当我刚加入 YouTube 时，我们的工作中 60% 是执行力，40% 是理解力。正确的。随着时间的推移，随着我们了解的越来越多，这种组合也会发生变化。现在我的团队可能执行 80%，20% 或 85% 以及 20% 到 15% 理解工作。 (00:32:18)：所以这不仅仅是写一个策略，而是说，好吧，如果我们有这些我们想要研究的主题，我们有信心知道什么，因为数据告诉我们，我们需要理解什么，因为我们没有数据，我们没有研究，我们没有见解？真正诚实地对待自己，哪些事情是低到中等的努力，但很有可能产生影响，因为你有数据，哪些事情你可能感兴趣，但因为你错过了一些东西，你错过了来自用户或数据的研究或反馈，或者一些见解或策略。你实际上应该说，我要先做这件事，然后再做其他事情。正确的。 (00:33:03)：这方面的一个例子是我的一个团队在 YouTube 上的现场体验中提供付费虚拟商品。这是一个非常非常重要且困难的问题空间。当我加入时，我们并没有真正完全了解整个实时生态系统，比如我们如何生活在这个实时生态系统中，我们的产品如何运作，最大的机会在哪里。因此，第一个也是最重要的理解工作不是将迭代交付到当前产品，而是需要真正了解正在发生的事情。正确的。比如每天有多少人观看直播，有多少人点击，有多少人看到我们的体验，有多少人真正购买？我们并没有真正充分地规划出经验，也没有了解差距在哪里，问题空间在哪里，我们应该关注哪里？ (00:33:52)：所以我们必须这样做。这就是理解多人、多个团队的工作。我们必须在工程方面做，我们需要数据科学作为分析。我们需要产品经理仔细回顾整个经历，找出问题所在。所有这些都是有意为之的，也是我们路线图上的可供性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's interesting about this is that this is very counterintuitive to how people would probably approach, hey, we need to speed up execution, we need to speed up growth, we need to ship more, execute, go faster, do more. And what you're saying is you find the impact comes from actually slow down how much we're doing and spend more time understanding to execute more intelligently.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，这与人们可能的做法非常违反直觉，嘿，我们需要加快执行速度，我们需要加快增长，我们需要运送更多，执行，走得更快，做得更多。你的意思是，你发现影响实际上来自于放慢我们正在做的事情，并花更多时间理解以更智能地执行。

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: That's right. Slow down and speed up.
turns.zh: 这是正确的。放慢速度并加快速度。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Fascinating. Because it's interesting, I have a bunch of questions that emerged out of folks that you've worked with and many of them are around how you turn a culture around, speed things up, and drive growth in a really meaningful way. And it sounds like this is one of your key strategies, is get people to spend more time understanding before diving into a bunch of stuff.
turns.zh: 迷人。因为这很有趣，我有很多与你共事过的人提出的问题，其中许多问题都围绕着你如何扭转一种文化，加快发展速度，并以一种真正有意义的方式推动增长。听起来这是你的关键策略之一，就是让人们在深入研究一堆东西之前花更多的时间来理解。

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: It does sound counterintuitive, but if you actually think about it, what is a better outcome? Is it a better outcome to just ship more faster now, but most of the things aren't unimpactful? Right. Or is it a better outcome to ship fewer things but really work on making sure that you're shipping them in the best way and de-risking a lot of other things so that a year later your win rate's higher and your velocity is higher?
turns.zh: 这听起来确实有悖常理，但如果你认真思考一下，什么是更好的结果呢？现在只是更快地发货是不是更好的结果，但大多数事情并非没有影响？正确的。或者，运送更少的东西，但真正努力确保以最佳方式运送它们，并降低许多其他东西的风险，以便一年后你的获胜率更高，你的速度更高，这是一个更好的结果吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I think counterintuitive is the wrong word. I think it makes sense. I think it's just no one does this. Usually everyone's like, move faster, we need more and ship more experiments.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为“反直觉”这个词是错误的。我认为这是有道理的。我认为只是没有人这样做。通常每个人都会说，行动得更快，我们需要更多并进行更多的实验。

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: Well, I mean this is the irony of growth, is people think growth is overnight success and it's not. Right. It is a lot of short wins and short-term execution for a longer-term gain and really understanding you have a lot of short terms towards the longer-term outcomes.
turns.zh: 嗯，我的意思是，这是增长的讽刺，人们认为增长是一夜成名，但事实并非如此。正确的。这是为了获得长期收益而进行的大量短期胜利和短期执行，并且真正了解您有很多短期目标来实现长期结果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So that people can take away this lesson, can you help people understand just when you say understand work, like what does that look like generally? Is it just a dedicated time to dive into data and answer a bunch of questions you've sent them? Is it running experiments to test hypotheses? What does that usually look like when you're, here let's do 40% understand work?
turns.zh: 为了让人们吸取这个教训，当你说理解工作时，你能帮助人们理解，就像一般情况下是什么样子吗？这只是专门的时间来深入研究数据并回答您发送给他们的一堆问题吗？是通过实验来检验假设吗？当你在这里让我们做 40% 的理解工作时，通常会是什么样子？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: The understand work sometimes comes from me, but most often comes from the teams themselves. And every function can do and should be doing understand work at some point. Right. And so it really depends on what the function is. So for an engineer, it could be looking at the code and saying, okay, we want to improve this. I need to do understand work to understand do we need to refactor this code and how scalable is it and what do we need to do to make sure that we can execute fast and make sure that we're not going to have a lot of start and stop? That could be understand work. It could be actually instrumenting the data and making sure that we actually have full visibility into what's going on. Data science, like we work a lot with data science doing activation metrics and understanding proxy metrics. Right. That's understand work because it helps us to figure out what we need to build and where to focus. (00:37:05): For product management, sometimes understand work is figuring out the partnership strategy ahead of actually launching the product because you need to go figure out how the pieces are going to come together. Right. And so it really just depends on what the function is. But when I say it should be coming from the bottoms up, what I mean is I encourage the team when we plan a sprint or plan a roadmap, to ask a question to identify the key themes that they need to work on. And when they ask a question on a key theme, also ask what else do we need to understand to make this happen? And in that planning session, to make sure that you are including cross-functional partners. So it's not just product design and data science and Inge, you also include go to market, you also include marketing because if you're not inclusive, then you don't really understand what the issues are.
turns.zh: 理解工作有时来自我，但大多数情况下来自团队本身。每个功能都可以并且应该在某个时候做理解工作。正确的。所以这实际上取决于功能是什么。因此，对于工程师来说，他可能会查看代码并说，好吧，我们想要改进它。我需要做一些理解工作，以了解我们是否需要重构此代码以及它的可扩展性如何，以及我们需要做什么来确保我们可以快速执行并确保我们不会有太多的启动和停止？这可能就是理解工作。它实际上可以对数据进行检测，并确保我们实际上能够完全了解正在发生的事情。数据科学，就像我们在数据科学方面做了很多工作一样，做激活指标和理解代理指标。正确的。这就是理解工作，因为它可以帮助我们弄清楚我们需要构建什么以及重点关注哪里。 (00:37:05)：对于产品管理，有时理解工作是在实际推出产品之前确定合作伙伴策略，因为您需要弄清楚各个部分如何组合在一起。正确的。所以这实际上只取决于功能是什么。但当我说它应该自下而上时，我的意思是我鼓励团队在计划冲刺或计划路线图时提出问题来确定他们需要研究的关键主题。当他们就一个关键主题提出问题时，还要问我们还需要了解什么才能实现这一目标？在该规划会议中，确保您包括跨职能合作伙伴。因此，这不仅仅是产品设计、数据科学和 Inge，还包括进入市场、营销，因为如果你不具有包容性，那么你就不会真正理解问题是什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: My PM brain is afraid of creating too much understand work and nothing getting done. How do you find that balance of we're going to be understanding for hours and days and weeks and months and not shipping much? How do you do some,-
turns.zh: 我的 PM 大脑害怕创建太多理解工作却一事无成。您如何找到我们需要数小时、数天、数周、数月的理解和不发货太多之间的平衡？你如何做一些，-

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: I tell them, you have to ship. I mean, you always have to ship, right? Sometimes I give them, sometimes it's helpful, especially early on because it takes a while for people to get their head around why this is so critical. I say, we should choose, sometimes I'll give them guidance. We should choose three to four understand projects that are going to really help this roadmap and figure out what they are. Right. So choose your top three or four and then let's talk about it. And I'll give them guidance. Or I would say figure out... There should always be some execution. So initially you're looking for low effort, high impact things to execute against. Right. (00:38:53): And so build a portfolio of work to do every sprint or every roadmap, some of which should be low effort, high impact, some of which should be medium effort, high impact. And sometimes understand work actually looks like doing a cheap test, doing a test that's going to help us to learn as fast as possible that we think is a good enough experience that can inform us. Right. And so identifying ways to do that. And so it's really about just managing expectations and helping people to be clear that the goal is to ship the product, but you want to ship the things that you have more confidence and understanding versus not.
turns.zh: 我告诉他们，你必须发货。我的意思是，你总是必须发货，对吗？有时我会给他们，有时这是有帮助的，尤其是在早期，因为人们需要一段时间才能理解为什么这如此重要。我说，我们应该选择，有时我会给他们指导。我们应该选择三到四个理解项目，这些项目将真正帮助这个路线图并弄清楚它们是什么。正确的。因此，请选择您的前三名或前四名，然后我们来讨论。我会给他们指导。或者我会说弄清楚……总应该有一些执行力。因此，最初您会寻找低工作量、高影响力的事情来执行。正确的。 (00:38:53)：因此，为每个冲刺或每个路线图建立一个工作组合，其中一些应该是低努力、高影响，其中一些应该是中等努力、高影响。有时，理解工作实际上看起来就像做一个廉价的测试，做一个测试将帮助我们尽可能快地学习，我们认为这是一个足够好的经验，可以为我们提供信息。正确的。因此找出实现这一目标的方法。因此，这实际上只是管理期望并帮助人们明确目标是交付产品，但你希望交付你更有信心和理解的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I think a big takeaway here is if you want to have more impact, move faster, try to spend a little more time understanding the problems you're going after in the opportunity space.
turns.zh: 因此，我认为这里的一个重要要点是，如果你想产生更大的影响，行动更快，尝试花更多的时间来理解你在机会空间中要解决的问题。

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: That's right. Right. I'll give you a very tactical example is when I joined Instagram in January 2016, believe it or not, the onboarding, the sign-up flow at Instagram had literally no logging to it. It had logging of how many people started and how many people ended. Right. And I joined in January and it was like we had to write a roadmap. And so the roadmap looked like this. Okay, we know this amount at the top of the funnel and this amount at the bottom end of the funnel. And there was eight steps in the funnel and we don't know what is going on. Right. So the first bit of understand work was we needed to do the instrumentation of that funnel as fast as possible to get the data to figure out where the drops were happening and what to fix. But because we knew of what was happening at the top of the funnel and the bottom of the funnel, we can go and play around with the experience and see what was broken. (00:40:32): So we ran a bunch of tests of stuff that was obviously broken to see what would improve. Right. And so it was like a mix. And so what we did was we set up time where we did, the beginning of like the first couple of weeks, add the logging, ship it to code, re-evaluate in the middle of the quarter, look at the full funnel and then add more things that we can do later on once we got that. But in order to get that done, that involved understand work with growth marketing to figure out what was the schemas for the instrumentation, right, the engineering to actually do that logging. Right. Data science to like pull together funnels and dashboard it, all of that had to come together all at one time.
turns.zh: 这是正确的。正确的。我会给你一个非常战术性的例子，当我在 2016 年 1 月加入 Instagram 时，不管你信不信，Instagram 的入职、注册流程实际上没有任何日志记录。它记录了有多少人开始和有多少人结束。正确的。我在一月份加入，就像我们必须写一个路线图一样。所以路线图看起来像这样。好的，我们知道漏斗顶部的数量和漏斗底端的数量。漏斗中有八个步骤，我们不知道发生了什么。正确的。因此，第一个理解工作是我们需要尽快对该漏斗进行检测，以获取数据来找出发生下降的位置以及需要修复的内容。但因为我们知道漏斗顶部和底部发生了什么，所以我们可以去尝试一下经验，看看哪里出了问题。 (00:40:32)：所以我们对明显有问题的东西进行了一系列测试，看看有什么可以改进的地方。正确的。所以这就像一个混合体。因此，我们所做的就是在我们所做的地方设置时间，就像前几周的开始一样，添加日志记录，将其发送到代码，在季度中期重新评估，查看完整的漏斗，然后添加更多我们稍后可以做的事情。但为了完成这一任务，需要了解与增长营销的合作，以弄清楚仪器的模式是什么，正确的，实际进行日志记录的工程。正确的。数据科学就像将漏斗整合在一起并用仪表板进行展示，所有这些都必须同时整合在一起。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really like just this concept of calling it understand work. I think that alone is a powerful tool because we're going to spend more time on understand work.
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢“理解工作”这个概念。我认为这本身就是一个强大的工具，因为我们将花更多的时间来理解工作。

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: It feels like it gives meaning to stuff that otherwise people would brush aside.
turns.zh: 感觉就像它赋予了人们会忽视的东西以意义。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right. Where it's just like, no, no, let's just ship stuff. Let's just try stuff. Let's just test the step. We'll see what happens.
turns.zh: 正确的。就像，不，不，我们只是运送东西。让我们尝试一下吧。我们来测试一下这个步骤。我们会看看会发生什么。

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 这是正确的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else you have seen and often do to help a team you join move faster and grow bigger? And I've heard that you've had a lot of impact on a lot of different cultures, so I'm curious if there's anything else that is really effective.
turns.zh: 您还见过或经常做其他什么事情来帮助您加入的团队更快地发展、壮大吗？我听说你对许多不同的文化产生了很大的影响，所以我很好奇是否还有其他真正有效的方法。

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: I've found myself in a bunch of interesting situations where I had to come in and help improve cultures or change cultures around teams. I found this framework, I don't even actually remember where I got it from, but it travels from computer to computer with me and team to team, and it's called managing complex change. I actually think I got it from business school or something. And it's really interesting. It's got these five components to it. There's vision, skills, incentives, resources, action plan, and you need all of those to have change. Right. Team needs to have vision, they need to have the skills, they need to have the right incentives. Sometimes some teams are incentivized to do some things versus others. You need to have the right resources in the right places and you need to have a clear action plan. And what I love about this framework is if you can visualize it and maybe you can share it with your podcast.
turns.zh: 我发现自己遇到了很多有趣的情况，我必须介入并帮助改善团队文化或改变团队文化。我发现了这个框架，我什至不记得我从哪里得到它，但它与我和团队一起从一台计算机传到另一台计算机，这就是所谓的管理复杂变更。我实际上认为我是从商学院或其他什么地方学到的。这真的很有趣。它有这五个组成部分。有愿景、技能、激励措施、资源、行动计划，你需要所有这些才能做出改变。正确的。团队需要有远见，需要有技能，需要有正确的激励。有时，一些团队会受到激励去做一些与其他团队不同的事情。您需要在正确的地方拥有正确的资源，并且需要有一个明确的行动计划。我喜欢这个框架的一点是，如果你可以将它可视化，也许你可以在你的播客中分享它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. We'll put it up on the screen on YouTube so folks can see what you're talking about.
turns.zh: 是的。我们会将其发布在 YouTube 的屏幕上，以便人们可以看到您在谈论的内容。

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: Basically what it does is it shows where if you're missing any one component, you get different outcomes. Right. So if you're missing the vision component, you end up in a state of confusion or if you're missing the incentives, you end up in a state of resistance because people aren't incentivized to do the right work. Or if you're missing an action plan, you end up in a state of false starts. So I use this, and I think about this a lot actually, because when you come in as a leader, as someone who's supposed to influence change, you have to really observe what's happening and figure out what are the challenges anecdotally and what are you observing? And then I figure out where I can plug in and what I can do to make the teams better. And what I tend to find is moving from the right side to the left side of this, like action plans are easier to institute. Right. (00:43:27): So if I see a team that's struggling to execute, I wonder do they have the right type of PRD framework or are they communicating well? Do they have the right type of team meeting structures? Those are kind of lower hanging fruit. It's a lot harder to change vision and skills. It will come in time. But what I also have done over the course of my career is I've built this deck that comes with me of different skills that matter. Right. What are different skills, what are different frameworks, how do we think about it, to help level teams fast? Right. Because I find that sometimes you walk in and not everyone is grounded in the same mental models or concepts. (00:44:07): One example of this I talk about a lot is Instagram. Instagram had just this fantastic culture of thinking about how do we ship high, high quality product, right, and what does product craft mean? And so that is something that I came to YouTube and my teams particularly, they didn't have a mental model for product craft. So I found myself talking into an echo chamber in some way. So I had to build a deck that showed, okay, here's how I think about product craft. Here's a framework for it. Here's how I think about all of these different things. And so now we have a shared language, shared communication for, and a repository of skills that we're going to build.
turns.zh: 基本上，它的作用是显示如果您缺少任何一个组件，您会得到不同的结果。正确的。因此，如果你缺少愿景，你最终会陷入混乱，或者如果你缺少激励，你最终会陷入抵制状态，因为人们没有动力去做正确的工作。或者，如果您缺少行动计划，您最终会陷入错误的开始状态。所以我使用这个，实际上我思考了很多，因为当你作为一个领导者，作为一个应该影响变革的人进来时，你必须真正观察正在发生的事情，并找出传闻中的挑战是什么以及你正在观察什么？然后我会弄清楚我可以在哪里加入以及我可以做些什么来让团队变得更好。我倾向于发现从右侧转向左侧，就像行动计划更容易制定一样。正确的。 (00:43:27)：因此，如果我看到一个团队难以执行，我想知道他们是否拥有正确类型的 PRD 框架，或者他们是否沟通良好？他们是否拥有正确类型的团队会议结构？这些都是唾手可得的成果。改变愿景和技能要困难得多。它会及时到来的。但在我的职业生涯中，我还制作了这套牌，它让我拥有了不同的重要技能。正确的。什么是不同的技能，什么是不同的框架，我们如何思考它，以帮助团队快速升级？正确的。因为我发现有时当你走进去时，并不是每个人都基于相同的心理模型或概念。 (00:44:07)：我经常谈论的一个例子是 Instagram。 Instagram 有着一种奇妙的文化，思考我们如何交付高品质的产品，对吧，产品工艺意味着什么？这就是我加入 YouTube 和我的团队的原因，特别是他们没有产品工艺的心智模型。所以我发现自己在某种程度上对着回音室说话。所以我必须建立一个展示，好吧，这就是我对产品工艺的看法。这是一个框架。以下是我对所有这些不同事物的看法。现在我们有了共同的语言、共同的沟通方式以及我们将要建立的技能库。

turns.en: I went to business school and I worked on Wall Street for a bit, and then I left my job on Wall Street, quit and started a startup. Startup was a glorious failure as many startups are, but it was like a very non-traditional path towards tech. And I think a lot of my time in these other industries actually shapes the way I think about products and product management and actually changing teams and building teams. And what I mean by that is I think there's a lot of similarities between education and product management believe it or not. (00:46:31): When I was interviewing for my first set of jobs in tech, recruiters would say to me, "How does your background relate? I don't really see it." And I would tell them, "When I was in education, I would walk into a classroom of 24, seven-year olds, and these kids owed me nothing. And the only way I could be successful or impactful is I needed to be able to be a strong communicator. I needed to be able to have a clear vision of what was going on. I needed to be able to influence them in a believable way such that they would get on board with what needed to be done for 270 days of the year." It's like when you walk into a room as a product manager, engineers, designers, researchers go to market. Nobody owes you anything. And the only thing that you're going to do in order to be successful is you need to be a strong communicator. You have a clear vision of what's going on and you need to be able to influence them to do the things together of what matters, right? It's very similar skillset, just different domain expertise. (00:47:29): And so because of that, right, I've really adopted a mindset of how do I coach my teams? How do I enable them? Because it's really about the sum of the parts versus me being a top down leader saying, you have to do this and you have to do that. And so I think a lot about that in both approach and the processes that we create. And to give you a couple of classic typical examples of this, there's two things I want to call out. One is there's this, actually this education framework, it's called Bloom's Taxonomy. I think it's changed over time, but when I learned it, it was basically a pyramid and the pyramid was, Bloom Taxonomy describes what's the different levels or order of critical thinking you need in order to be a master of something? And at the bottom of the pyramid was knowledge, and then it's comprehension, and then application, analysis, synthesis, and evaluation. Right. (00:48:26): And so going up the pyramid, it means it's higher order thinking. And I think about that a lot and trying to understand where are my teams struggling? Do they have the core knowledge that they need? Do they understand it but they can't apply it or they apply it, but they're not able to analyze it across different business segments? Right. And you can use this framework not only with the ICPMs and the teams themselves, but also for your managers, like what is breaking down? And in using that and attaching that to the skills that we want to build to figure out how do you fill in those gaps? Right. And it really is a grounding for me, a grounding mental model for how do you build teams that are actually affect them? How do you meet people where they are as opposed to just saying, hey, you need to figure this out? Right. I find that too often in tech and also in product, people are ask to figure things out but not given the support to get there, and there's no way to really connect the dots for them.
turns.zh: 我去了商学院，在华尔街工作了一段时间，然后我辞去了华尔街的工作，辞职并创办了一家初创公司。与许多初创公司一样，初创公司是一次光荣的失败，但这就像一条非常非传统的科技之路。我认为我在这些其他行业的很多时间实际上塑造了我对产品和产品管理的思考方式，以及实际上改变团队和建设团队的方式。我的意思是，无论你信不信，我认为教育和产品管理之间有很多相似之处。 (00:46:31)：当我面试第一套科技工作时，招聘人员会对我说，“你的背景有什么关系？我真的不明白。”我会告诉他们，“当我从事教育工作时，我会走进一个由 24 岁、7 岁孩子组成的教室，这些孩子不欠我任何东西。我取得成功或产生影响力的唯一方法是我需要能够成为一名强有力的沟通者。我需要能够对正在发生的事情有一个清晰的愿景。我需要能够以一种可信的方式影响他们，以便他们能够参与一年中 270 天需要做的事情。”这就像当你走进一个房间时，产品经理、工程师、设计师、研究人员正在走向市场。没有人欠你任何东西。为了获得成功，你唯一要做的就是成为一名强大的沟通者。您对正在发生的事情有清晰的认识，并且您需要能够影响他们一起做重要的事情，对吗？它们的技能非常相似，只是领域专业知识不同。 (00:47:29)：正因为如此，我真的采取了一种如何指导我的团队的心态？我如何启用它们？因为这实际上是各个部分的总和，而不是我作为一个自上而下的领导者说，你必须这样做，你必须这样做。因此，我在我们创建的方法和流程中对此进行了很多思考。为了给大家提供几个经典的典型例子，我想指出两件事。一个是这个，实际上是这个教育框架，它被称为布鲁姆分类法。我认为它随着时间的推移而改变，但当我学习它时，它基本上是一个金字塔，金字塔是，布鲁姆分类法描述了成为某事物的大师所需的批判性思维的不同级别或顺序是什么？金字塔的最底层是知识，然后是理解，然后是应用、分析、综合、评价。正确的。 (00:48:26)：沿着金字塔往上走，意味着更高层次的思维。我经常思考这个问题，并试图了解我的团队在哪里苦苦挣扎？他们是否拥有所需的核心知识？他们是否理解但无法应用，或者应用但无法跨不同业务部门进行分析？正确的。您不仅可以将这个框架用于 ICPM 和团队本身，还可以用于您的经理，例如发生了什么故障？在使用它并将其附加到我们想要培养的技能中，以找出如何填补这些空白？正确的。这对我来说确实是一个基础，一个关于如何建立真正影响他们的团队的基础心理模型？你如何与人们见面，而不是只是说，嘿，你需要弄清楚这一点？正确的。我发现，在技术和产品中，人们经常被要求解决问题，但没有得到实现这一目标的支持，而且没有办法真正为他们连接点。

What are some of the other things that often you find that maybe hinder a product manager's success?
turns.zh: 惊人的。我正在提取布鲁姆分类法。因此，本质上，如果你看到一位产品经理陷入困境，你要做的就是找出他们没有哪些东西？你怎么不支持他们呢？你怎样才能更好地支持他们？所以可能是他们没有技能，他们没有理解力。您经常发现哪些其他因素可能会阻碍产品经理的成功？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: A lot of times they might have the understanding, but they haven't had a chance to apply it to a variety of different scenarios or haven't seen it applied to multiple scenarios. Right. So oftentimes you might understand a concept like machine learning, but you haven't actually worked on it in against multiple scenarios. So you maybe have one way of doing it that doesn't make sense and you need to have two or three, and you don't even know that two or three ways of doing it exists. Right. That is often a common failure point. Right. Or it's maybe you know how to apply it, but you can't synthesize why this thing that you're doing actually matters for the business context. Right. Oftentimes that becomes a challenge with managers. It's like they know what to do, but they don't understand how to tie it back to the business context and the overall strategy needs and so where to prioritize. Right. (00:50:31): And so what I find is that when you're trying to manage managers, you're really trying to live at the top of the pyramid. You are responsible, managers responsible for basically owning that pyramid for all of the areas that they operate, but they need to be able to live at the top of the pyramid across all of them. They need to be able to synthesize and evaluate what's happening for each product team that they own in order to kind of make the bigger picture connections.
turns.zh: 很多时候他们可能有了理解，但是他们没有机会将其应用到各种不同的场景中，或者没有看到它应用到多种场景中。正确的。很多时候，你可能理解了机器学习这样的概念，但你并没有真正针对多种场景进行过研究。因此，您可能有一种没有意义的方法，而您需要两种或三种方法，而您甚至不知道存在两种或三种方法。正确的。这通常是一个常见的故障点。正确的。或者也许您知道如何应用它，但您无法综合为什么您正在做的事情实际上对业务环境很重要。正确的。这常常成为管理者面临的挑战。就好像他们知道要做什么，但不知道如何将其与业务环境和整体战略需求联系起来，也不知道优先考虑的事项。正确的。 (00:50:31)：所以我发现，当你试图管理管理者时，你实际上是在努力生活在金字塔的顶端。你是负责的，管理者负责基本上拥有他们经营的所有领域的金字塔，但他们需要能够生活在所有领域的金字塔的顶部。他们需要能够综合和评估他们拥有的每个产品团队正在发生的事情，以便建立更大的联系。

turns.en: One thing that I also think about a lot, and I don't know if this is just a me thing, but I think about PM as a team sport. Right. Leading product teams is really about...
turns.zh: 我也思考了很多事情，我不知道这是否只是我个人的事情，但我认为 PM 作为一项团队运动。正确的。领导产品团队实际上是……

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: Leading product teams is really about being the coach and helping other people to see what their role is on the team and to maximize them. People talk a lot about product as you're the CEO, and I don't actually fully believe that analogy. If you think about it as a team sport, there's a few things that shake out. One is not everyone's going to be a star player. But not everyone needs to be a LeBron James or Kobe Bryant. You need role players. You need really strong role players. You need people who feel valued in their role, and you need to understand how to groom those role players and how to make sure that they have the right seat at the table and the right place. So I think it's, yes, you're the conductor of the orchestra, but you're really more than that. You're really the coach of the team. (00:52:46): Another thing I think about a lot is I have a good friend who's a college basketball coach, and he taught me about this idea of your coaching tree. This is a really important concept, especially in college basketball. You, as a head coach, you take a lot of pride in who are your assistants. Who is your first assistant, second assistant, and third assistant? And where do they go on to be head coaches? And what legacy do they have because you were able to instill a bit in them? The coaching tree of a Mike Mike Krzyzewski, the coaching tree of a John Calipari, these esteemed coaches, not only because of what they've done, but because of the tree that they've built. (00:53:26): And I like to think about this as well, because I think it's really important for product leaders, think about what is their leadership tree. Who have you helped to build up and help to grow and help to get to their next wall? And so I think about this a lot. I have people who I've worked with who are running growth at Stripe or the CPO at Chief or now running stories at Instagram that were on my team in the earlier days. And their success is my success, and I'm proud for them, and I'm happy for them. And I think it kind of reinforces this mentality that it's your responsibility to coach people up to greatness.
turns.zh: 领导产品团队实际上就是充当教练，帮助其他人了解他们在团队中的角色并最大限度地发挥他们的作用。当你是首席执行官时，人们会谈论很多产品，但我实际上并不完全相信这个类比。如果你将其视为一项团队运动，就会发现一些事情会发生变化。一是不是每个人都会成为明星球员。但并不是每个人都需要成为勒布朗·詹姆斯或科比·布莱恩特。你需要角色扮演者。你需要非常强大的角色扮演者。你需要那些感觉自己的角色受到重视的人，你需要了解如何培养这些角色扮演者，以及如何确保他们在谈判桌上拥有正确的席位和正确的位置。所以我认为，是的，你是乐团的指挥，但你的意义远不止于此。你确实是球队的教练。 (00:52:46)：我经常思考的另一件事是我有一个好朋友，他是一名大学篮球教练，他教了我关于教练树的想法。这是一个非常重要的概念，尤其是在大学篮球中。作为一名主教练，你对自己的助理教练感到非常自豪。你的第一助理、第二助理、第三助理是谁？他们将在哪里担任主教练？因为你能够向他们灌输一些东西，所以他们有什么遗产？迈克·沙舍夫斯基的教练树，约翰·卡利帕里的教练树，这些受人尊敬的教练，不仅因为他们所做的事情，还因为他们建立的教练树。 (00:53:26)：我也喜欢思考这个问题，因为我认为这对于产品领导者来说非常重要，想想他们的领导力树是什么。你帮助谁建立、成长并帮助他们到达下一堵墙？所以我经常思考这个问题。我的一些同事曾在 Stripe 负责增长工作，或者在 Chief 担任 CPO，或者现在在 Instagram 负责故事，这些人都是我早期团队中的成员。他们的成功就是我的成功，我为他们感到骄傲，为他们感到高兴。我认为这强化了这种心态：你有责任指导人们走向伟大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what I'm hearing is you put a lot of value in your team on them coaching folks, whether they're managers or even ICs is helping them understand that it's important to coach folks on their team and help them develop, that it's part of your job, essentially.
turns.zh: 所以我听到的是，你在团队中非常重视对员工的指导，无论他们是经理还是 IC，帮助他们理解指导团队成员并帮助他们发展是很重要的，这本质上是你工作的一部分。

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: That's part of your job. You are trying to build a repository of skills and repository of knowledge and of team velocity. And the only way you can do that is everyone is... So rising tide has to lift all boats.

turns.zh: 嗯，你真是太慷慨了。我不会说，看，我们已经做了一些非常好的工作，到目前为止在 YouTube 上做了一些很好的工作，这是一个旅程。我确实对飞轮思考了很多。我认为，真正的增长在于真正理解什么是价值利润、所有不同的体验点，特别是如果你有一个多边市场。 YouTube 的多边市场就像创作者以及创作者试图实现的目标，无论是从参与角度来看，还是从盈利角度来看。那么对于观众或购买者来说，他们的帽子在哪里？他们想做什么？他们在哪里错过了机会？ (00:56:13)：我无法详细讨论 YouTube 的细节，但我想说的是，我进来时总是做的一件事是，如果你愿意的话，我会尝试推动我的团队在其相邻的用户状态下提供真正的狗粮产品。我的意思是，你我使用多年的产品实际上并不是我们为其他人构建的产品。就像使用某个产品的高级用户一样...有太多的历史和关于该产品如何...的丰富知识...该产品实际上为您创造了良好的体验，如果您今天去创建一个新的 Gmail 帐户并观看 YouTube，我向您保证，这将是一次完全不同且明显更糟糕的体验。 (00:57:03)：并且错过了很多明显的机会，尤其是飞轮是什么，以及如果您不真正在新状态下使用东西，为什么东西会起作用或不起作用。当我们谈论 YouTube 时，一个这样的例子是，很多用于搜索内容的 YouTube 图表都是基于您过去观看过的内容？因此，如果你去搜索并搜索历史记录，那么你过去看过什么或搜索过什么，我们可以向你展示什么是我们可以更好地预测的？ (00:57:33)：但是如果你没有一行搜索历史记录，那么他们就不会做得那么好。所以这并不是我们正在做的事情的直接翻译。但对我来说，我致力于自由货币化，创作者如何制作可以帮助他们货币化的内容，确实存在非常重要的飞轮？我们如何向人们提供这些内容，我们在多大程度上向人们提供这些内容，以及我们如何确保人们对他们所收到的内容和付费的人感觉良好。所有这些飞轮都必须工作。 (00:58:02)：所以我能做的一部分就是真正思考如何将故事中的各个点联系起来，让团队可以独特地理解，可以帮助他们更加深入，并明确工作目标。有时，飞轮最重要的实际上是让您的团队知道该做什么、不该做什么。然后，它还可以帮助我们了解关于创作者和观众以及货币化操作我们知道什么和不知道什么，以便我们可以进行理解工作以提高速度并证明影响。 (00:58:35)：这确实是我们一直关注的焦点。所以我在 YouTube 上做了很多这样的事情，但我也在 Instacart 上做了同样的事情，认真思考当我加入 Instacart 时，我遇到的一个大问题是，人们在日常生活中会如何......他们的日常生活实际上如何反映在购买体验中？我们是否让他们变得容易？因为当您购买杂货时，您不会因为想要冰箱里有漂亮的食材而去杂货店购物。你去杂货店购物是因为你实际上有一顿饭要准备。那么，我们实际上是否反映了要完成的真正工作，即我想买炸玉米饼，我想星期二做炸玉米饼。我们能否让人们更容易地找到炸玉米饼的原料，而不是让他们分类玉米饼、西红柿和鳄梨？因此，我们真正思考的是工作是什么，然后实现这一目标的飞轮是什么，以及我们如何使其成为现实？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: This was something that came out of actually my time at Instagram. It was a framework that we came up with because Instagram really was, at that time, we grew so fast that the people who were using Instagram in February were completely different than people who were using it the following October and then the next January. I think when I joined, we were at like 440 million monthly actives. January 2016, at the end of that year we were at 636 million, grew like 47% that year. Literally people said that, it was that long ago. And then a year later it's like, "Of course I use Instagram. Instagram is my everything." The world changed so fast. (01:04:21): And so when you're in a hypergrowth product, it's really, really important to understand who your users are today and the persona of the user, what motivates them, why they're using it, but then also to understand who is the next user? Who is the user who could be using this product, but for some reason it doesn't work for them, and understanding who that adjacent user is and when you are actually starting to see that adjacent user adopt the product. And one of the ways you start to see the adjacent users starting to adopt the product, especially with the data, is you start seeing cohort curves decline. You start seeing the people who sign up today, three or six months from now, they're signing up and they're doing a worse job. Nothing's changing the product, but just the understanding of how the product should work is different. (01:05:12): They might be less tech savvy. On a scale of an early adopter versus late majority, they might be closer to the late majority. And so we saw this at Instagram. We always knew working on our registration flow, and at one point we were converting at some insanely high percent, and then three months later it would go down by 15%, not because anything was broken, but just because we'd broken into new markets. You bring on people in India or you bring on people in the Philippines, and their understanding of how it works, the phones they use, et cetera are all different. So really, the core of their adjacent news was a few things. One is like you have to understand who's using your product today and why. And when you're growing at some really strong pace, 30, 40, 50% or more per year, you've got to be on top of who you believe the next user is and why. (01:06:02): And then you also have to be the adjacent exactly, use the product like them and see how it's working, what's broken with it. And so at an Instacart, the adjacent user, the original user might've been like an office admin who is going to buy this thing every week because of during happy hours and team staff. But then the next adjacent user might've been the mom of three or four or the dad of three or four who's home with the kids and they need to depend on Instacart, versus later on it might be they're a single person in New York who does this out of convenience. But what they're optimizing for, how they use the product all changes, and the functionality and the abilities are fundamentally different. So you have to be them, you have to watch how they use the product, you have to talk to them, and then have to visit them and literally see what they're doing in real time in order to make sure that you're enabling the right jobs for them.
turns.zh: 这其实是我在 Instagram 的经历中产生的。这是我们提出的一个框架，因为当时 Instagram 确实发展得很快，二月份使用 Instagram 的人与第二年 10 月和第二年 1 月使用它的人完全不同。我想当我加入时，我们的月活跃用户数约为 4.4 亿。 2016 年 1 月，当年年底我们的用户数量达到 6.36 亿，当年增长了 47%。因此，当我们与 2016 年上半年的用户交谈时，当我们与 30 岁的美国女性交谈时，她们会说，“我为什么要有 Instagram？我有 Facebook 帐户。”人们确实这么说，那是很久以前的事了。一年后，我会说：“我当然使用 Instagram。Instagram 就是我的一切。”世界变化太快了。 (01:04:21)：因此，当您使用高速增长的产品时，了解您今天的用户是谁以及用户的角色、他们的动机是什么、他们为什么使用该产品非常非常重要，但也要了解谁是下一个用户？谁是可以使用该产品的用户，但由于某种原因它对他们不起作用，并了解该相邻用户是谁以及您何时真正开始看到该相邻用户采用该产品。你开始看到相邻用户开始采用该产品的方式之一，特别是通过数据，你开始看到队列曲线下降。你开始看到今天注册的人，三到六个月后，他们注册了，但他们的工作却变得更糟。产品没有发生任何改变，只是对产品如何工作的理解有所不同。 (01:05:12)：他们可能不太懂技术。从早期采用者与晚期多数的规模来看，他们可能更接近晚期多数。我们在 Instagram 上看到了这一点。我们一直都知道如何处理我们的注册流程，有一次我们的转化率达到了惊人的高水平，然后三个月后，它会下降 15%，不是因为任何东西出了问题，而只是因为我们打入了新市场。你请来印度的人，或者请来菲律宾的人，他们对它的工作原理的理解、他们使用的手机等等都是不同的。事实上，他们相邻新闻的核心是几件事。一是你必须了解今天谁在使用你的产品以及为什么。当您以每年 30%、40%、50% 或更高的速度快速增长时，您必须了解您认为下一个用户是谁以及原因。 (01:06:02)：然后你还必须准确地相邻，像他们一样使用产品，看看它是如何工作的，有什么问题。因此，在 Instacart 中，相邻用户、原始用户可能就像办公室管理员一样，由于欢乐时光和团队工作人员的原因，他每周都会购买这个东西。但下一个相邻的用户可能是三四个孩子的妈妈，或者是三四个孩子的爸爸，他们在家带孩子，他们需要依赖 Instacart，而后来他们可能是纽约的单身人士，出于方便而这样做。但他们优化的目的、使用产品的方式都发生了变化，而且功能和能力也根本不同。所以你必须成为他们，你必须观察他们如何使用产品，你必须与他们交谈，然后必须拜访他们并实时了解他们在做什么，以确保你为他们提供合适的工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love just the visualization of the adjacent user. Basically your growth is going to come from non-existing users. It's the users right outside that circle of...
turns.zh: 我喜欢相邻用户的可视化效果。基本上你的增长将来自不存在的用户。是那个圈子之外的用户......

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 这是正确的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... pre-users are today, and you need to think about what do they need that existing users maybe don't need. You said that this is most powerful for hypergrowth companies. Is this something you think people like all companies should be thinking about or is it a lot less important if you're not a hypergrowth business?
turns.zh: ...今天是预用户，您需要考虑他们需要哪些现有用户可能不需要的东西。你说这对于高速增长的公司来说是最强大的。您认为这是像所有公司一样的人们都应该考虑的事情吗？还是说，如果您不是一家高速增长的企业，那么这一点就不那么重要了？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: So it's a great question. I think it's essential. It's mandatory for hypergrowth. I think it's very helpful if you have a product or a company that is not growing what you want it to be. And so you are focused on capturing more share of wallet instead of expanding your audience. And so sometimes you can imagine a cosmetics company, for example, that's like digitally enabled. You can imagine that they've hit a ceiling in terms of the growth of their users, and they're really just trying to get people to buy more product, but maybe the people who want to use their product are missing something from your current product. Maybe you're missing different skin tone shades, or maybe you're missing certain types of tools. So really talking to who is just outside of your current user base, who's coming to your product and looking around and not buying and understanding what are their needs and figuring out how do you enable for them, how do you build the right experience for them in order to become adopters of your product?
turns.zh: 所以这是一个很好的问题。我认为这是必要的。这是高速增长所必需的。我认为，如果您的产品或公司没有按照您的预期发展，这将非常有帮助。因此，您的重点是获得更多的钱包份额，而不是扩大受众群体。因此，有时您可以想象一家化妆品公司，例如，这家公司就像是数字化的。你可以想象他们的用户增长已经达到了上限，他们实际上只是想让人们购买更多的产品，但也许想要使用他们产品的人缺少你当前产品的某些东西。也许您缺少不同的肤色色调，或者您可能缺少某些类型的工具。因此，真正与那些不属于您当前用户群的人交谈，谁会来到您的产品并环顾四周，而不是购买并了解他们的需求，并弄清楚如何为他们提供支持，如何为他们构建正确的体验，以便成为您产品的采用者？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what I'm hearing is spend some understand work to figure out who your potential users are,
turns.zh: 所以我听到的是花一些理解工作来找出你的潜在用户是谁，

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 这是正确的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... and then use the product as them and see what is missing. I imagine user research goes into this. You're not actually going to understand necessarily all the things they need. So it's probably fine folks in that cohort and see how they use the product. Awesome.
turns.zh: ...然后像他们一样使用该产品，看看缺少什么。我想用户研究会涉及到这一点。你实际上不一定能理解他们需要的所有东西。因此，这可能是该群体中的好人，看看他们如何使用该产品。惊人的。

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: The question I had on my mind as you're talking, you've come into so many companies and helped them with growth. Where do you find most of the opportunities often lie? Is it like onboarding, activation? Is there a trend like that you're like, "Here's probably there's going to be opportunity here," or is it super mixed bag?
turns.zh: 当你说话时，我脑子里浮现的问题是，你加入了很多公司并帮助他们成长。您发现大多数机会通常在哪里？类似于入职、激活吗？是否存在这样的趋势，“这里可能会有机会”，或者是超级混合包？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: Usually it's somewhere in the onboarding to habit-building experience. What does it take for someone to actually understand the value, that first moment, that first aha moment in the product? And a lot of teams, it's shocking how many teams don't really understand what that moment is for them. And then also how do you get them to build habit around the product. Oftentimes, a lot of people equate growth to top of funnel, and that is also critical. I think having the right top of funnel motion is really critical and building on that. So I think there's one part of, it's like once you have the right top of funnel motion to get people to come in, how do you help to make sure of the defining value and the building habit and their routine? Because that's the thing that helps you to compound over time. If you're bringing a lot of people but they're not staying around, then you just have a leaky bucket and it doesn't matter how big your top funnel is. So making sure that that first-month and two-month, three-month experience is great. (01:10:04): And then the other part is really figuring out how do you build compounding growth loops where it's not just one way of acquiring people, but you're building two and three and four ways that layer onto each other that help you to really supercharge your engine of acquiring people. So at Instagram, if you kind of look at where Instagram is and how I [inaudible 01:10:28] and grew, there's a lot that goes into it, but if you actually unpack the top of funnel for what worked at Instagram, there's certainly a component of it, which was our core component, which was invitations, where people inviting you and making sure that those invitations work and they work well and that people, their friends are coming on, you get notified. (01:10:48): But another part that goes unspoken, still critical to this day was the celebrity partnerships was critical, because basically they had this wonderful partnerships team that basically took Instagram and taught celebrities how to use it, how to make it work for them, how to tell their own story and be their own brand, and that was a critical growth funnel because with that, you had the ability for them to create these celebrities and celebrity creators to set the norm for how the platform gets used, but they also were getting picked up by the news and the media for all the stuff that's happening in the celebrity world, which then added onto this other growth level, which was SEO. (01:11:36): And so every time a news article came out, they would link to the creators or the celebrities Instagram account or that particular post. And so you have this whole SEO engine that worked. And the SEO engine was because you have both web, which we launched at Instagram, which created the canonical SEO tables, and then you had all of these inbound links from these celebrity sites and news media, but then what you also had is you had embeds for Instagram and all of these different sites, like a news article, whatever, the posts, Lenny's podcast, Instagram account, and those embeds help with SEO juice. (01:12:15): And so you have not just the invites, but now you have the celebrities, now you have the SEO component. And then we would do a bunch of paid media on top of that using a lot of those signals. And then we have our own content. And so you would have all of these different growth engines compounding each other. So every time the invitations got better, every time we've got more celebrities, every time SEO gets better, it's like magnifying the top of funnel, and at the bottom of the funnel or mid-funnel, making sure that people are retaining and getting value and staying around over the long term.
turns.zh: 通常它是在习惯养成过程中的某个地方。人们需要怎样才能真正理解产品的价值，即第一个时刻，第一个顿悟时刻？对于很多团队来说，令人震惊的是有多少团队并不真正了解那一刻对他们来说意味着什么。然后还有如何让他们养成围绕产品的习惯。很多时候，很多人将增长等同于漏斗顶部，这也很重要。我认为拥有漏斗运动的右顶部非常重要，并在此基础上建立。所以我认为有一部分，就像一旦你有了漏斗运动的正确顶部来让人们进来，你如何帮助确保定义价值和建立习惯及其日常工作？因为这可以帮助你随着时间的推移而复合。如果你带来了很多人，但他们没有留下来，那么你只是一个漏桶，不管你的顶部漏斗有多大。因此，确保第一个月、两个月、三个月的体验非常棒。 (01:10:04)：另一部分是真正弄清楚如何建立复合增长循环，这不仅仅是一种吸引人才的方式，而是建立两种、三种和四种相互叠加的方式，帮助你真正增强吸引人才的引擎。因此，在 Instagram，如果你看看 Instagram 的定位以及我 [听不清 01:10:28] 和成长的情况，就会发现有很多内容，但如果你真正了解 Instagram 的漏斗顶部，肯定有一个组成部分，这是我们的核心组成部分，即邀请，人们邀请你并确保这些邀请有效，并且效果良好，并且人们、他们的朋友来了，你会收到通知。 (01:10:48)：但另一个不言而喻的部分，至今仍然至关重要，名人合作伙伴关系至关重要，因为基本上他们有一个出色的合作伙伴团队，基本上以 Instagram 为基础，教名人如何使用它，如何让它为他们服务，如何讲述自己的故事并成为自己的品牌，这是一个关键的增长漏斗，因为有了这个，你就有能力让他们创造这些名人和名人创作者，为平台的使用方式设定规范，但他们也被新闻和媒体报道名人世界中发生的所有事情，然后添加到另一个增长水平，即搜索引擎优化。 (01:11:36)：因此每次发布新闻文章时，他们都会链接到创作者或名人的 Instagram 帐户或该特定帖子。这样你就拥有了整个 SEO 引擎。 SEO 引擎是因为你同时拥有我们在 Instagram 上推出的网络，它创建了规范的 SEO 表，然后你拥有来自这些名人网站和新闻媒体的所有入站链接，但你还拥有 Instagram 和所有这些不同网站的嵌入内容，例如新闻文章等，帖子、Lenny 的播客、Instagram 帐户，以及这些有助于 SEO 效果的嵌入内容。 (01:12:15)：因此，您不仅拥有邀请，还拥有名人，现在您拥有 SEO 组件。然后我们会使用大量这些信号来制作一堆付费媒体。然后我们就有了自己的内容。因此，所有这些不同的增长引擎都会相互复合。因此，每次邀请变得更好，每次我们有更多的名人，每次搜索引擎优化变得更好，这就像放大漏斗的顶部，以及漏斗的底部或漏斗中部，确保人们保留并获得价值并长期留在身边。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is so interesting. I had no idea this was such a core part of the early growth strategy. Everyone's always talking about reality and word of mouth, all these things. And you're saying partnerships was a key part of the early growth strategy.
turns.zh: 那太有趣了。我不知道这是早期增长战略的核心部分。每个人总是在谈论现实和口碑，所有这些事情。您说合作伙伴关系是早期增长战略的关键部分。

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: Huge. It's huge.
turns.zh: 巨大的。它是巨大的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's so funny. Never something people talk about in growth, this partnership. It's always is like, "Oh, there's a couple of companies that really had success from partnerships in BD." How early was this a big part of the strategy? How early in the history of,
turns.zh: 太有趣了。人们从来不谈论成长、这种伙伴关系。人们总是会说，“哦，有几家公司确实通过 BD 合作取得了成功。”这是该战略的重要组成部分有多早？历史有多早，

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: I mean the partnerships team was there before I joined. It was a very savvy and astute thing that Kevin and Mikey set up. The partnerships team drove a lot of the word of mouth around Instagram, but it was the partnership's work in combination with the product work that actually helped to allow a lot of that to land. It was our ability to think outside the box and understand that we needed to have a web presence because it was critical for international growth and it also helped with SEO. And so the idea of launching web really drove and actually increased Instagram's growth by 10% the minute we launched it. And it was something that George Wang, who was there before me, had the idea around. It wasn't really something that Kevin and Mikey believed in initially, but we had to prove to them that it was really impactful and one should launch. (01:14:03): Then they understood why it was impactful and all of the effect of it. But web was really critical for driving so much SEO, which helped support a lot of the celebrity work and the partnerships work, because now every time creator or celebrity did something on Instagram, every news media article picked it up and it just helped to drive searches in Google searches, which helped to make Instagram part of the cultural zeitgeist.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，在我加入之前，合作伙伴团队就已经在那里了。这是凯文和米奇非常精明和精明的做法。合作伙伴团队在 Instagram 上带来了很多口碑，但实际上是合作伙伴的工作与产品工作相结合，才真正帮助了很多口碑的落地。这是我们跳出框框思考的能力，并了解我们需要拥有网络存在，因为这对于国际增长至关重要，并且也有助于搜索引擎优化。因此，推出网络版的想法确实推动了 Instagram 的增长，实际上，在我们推出 Instagram 的那一刻起，它就实现了 10% 的增长。这是乔治·王（George Wang）在我之前提出的想法。 Kevin 和 Mikey 最初并不真正相信这一点，但我们必须向他们证明它确实有影响力并且应该推出。 (01:14:03)：然后他们明白了为什么它有影响力以及它的所有影响。但网络对于推动如此多的 SEO 确实至关重要，这有助于支持许多名人的工作和合作伙伴关系的工作，因为现在每次创作者或名人在 Instagram 上做某事时，每一篇新闻媒体文章都会报道它，并且它只是有助于推动 Google 搜索中的搜索，这有助于使 Instagram 成为文化时代精神的一部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is so interesting, because everyone imagines Instagram, virality, word of mouth, like SEO and partnerships sounds like a core part of Instagram's early growth, which I don't think anyone ever talks about.
turns.zh: 这很有趣，因为每个人都认为 Instagram、病毒式传播、口碑传播、搜索引擎优化和合作伙伴关系听起来像是 Instagram 早期发展的核心部分，但我认为没有人谈论过这一点。

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: No, that's huge.
turns.zh: 不，那是巨大的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。
