turns.en: I mean it was part of Facebook's growth too, but I think a little bit differently. It's not as much partnership, but when you Google someone now, you Google someone's name, oftentimes, Instagram is one of the first five things that comes up for the average person,
turns.zh: 我的意思是，这也是 Facebook 增长的一部分，但我的想法有点不同。这并不是什么合作关系，但当你现在用谷歌搜索某人时，你用谷歌搜索某人的名字，通常，Instagram 是普通人首先想到的五件事之一，

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, right.
turns.zh: 是的，对。

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: ... now, by design.
turns.zh: ...现在，按照设计。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: LinkedIn, Instagram, Twitter.
turns.zh: 领英、Instagram、推特。

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 这是正确的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you ever see the video of Alex Jiu talking about TikTok's growth strategy of this whole... He had this metaphor, and he was trying to grow off of Instagram, so his metaphor was Instagram is like you're in Europe and you're killing it. If you're in Europe and you're king, you don't ever want to go to America. There's no reason for you to give it up. And America is TikTok in this case. He's like, "How do we convince people to come to America and try moving everything there?" He's like, "We need to go after the people that are not doing well in Europe, who want to be the king, and we're going to help you become that king in America, or the President."
turns.zh: 你有没有看过 Alex Jiu 谈论 TikTok 整个增长战略的视频……他有一个比喻，他试图在 Instagram 上发展壮大，所以他的比喻是 Instagram 就像你在欧洲，你正在杀死它。如果你在欧洲并且你是国王，你就永远不想去美国。你没有理由放弃它。在这种情况下，美国就是 TikTok。他说，“我们如何说服人们来到美国并尝试将所有东西搬到那里？”他说，“我们需要追捕那些在欧洲表现不佳、想成为国王的人，我们将帮助你成为美国的国王，或者总统。”

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: So he used the adjacent... Used that theory on us, basically, is what you're saying.
turns.zh: 所以他使用了相邻的...在我们身上使用了这个理论，基本上就是你所说的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's right. He did. Drink up your shake.
turns.zh: 这是正确的。他做到了。喝完你的奶昔。

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Yeah. And I think the reason that strategy worked differently is there was already a place, so they couldn't execute what you did because there's already celebrities already there, and it's not like, "Come here." There's no point. I already have a huge following.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为策略效果不同的原因是已经有一个地方了，所以他们无法执行你所做的事情，因为那里已经有名人了，而这并不像“来这里”。没有意义。我已经拥有了大量的追随者。

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: So you make your own celebrities.
turns.zh: 所以你创造了自己的名人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Make your own celebrities. Exactly. And they went after the B-list, C-list people. So it's interesting that people look at Instagram, like, cool, we're going to do partnerships, SEO. But I think it's important to realize things change when the market is a different dynamic. You can't just do the same thing.
turns.zh: 打造自己的名人。确切地。他们追随二流、三流的人。所以有趣的是，人们看着 Instagram，就像，很酷，我们将进行合作伙伴关系、搜索引擎优化。但我认为，当市场出现不同的动态时，认识到事情会发生变化是很重要的。你不能只做同样的事情。

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 这是正确的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It won't work as well. Is there anything else from the Instagram early days that maybe people wouldn't know or would be interesting to share? Because you were there quite early, and now it's maybe the most thriving social network in the world.
turns.zh: 它也不会起作用。 Instagram 早期还有哪些人们可能不知道或有兴趣分享的东西吗？因为你很早就在那里了，现在它可能是世界上最繁荣的社交网络。

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: One thing that's actually, I think, interesting, as an interesting story that doesn't get talked about a lot is I think the early Instagram was built where... it was built in a way where every follow was created equal. And what I mean by that is if I followed you, Lenny, or if I followed Kim Kardashian, I followed Selena Gomez, all follows were treated like they were equally important. And this is actually a really important fact. It was a really important factor for a couple of reasons. One, early celebrities who were adopting Instagram obviously benefited from that, because a celebrity is going to get a follow before an average person does. It doesn't mean that their followers weren't meaningful. It's just that when you have a machine learning that's just optimized for a click through a follow, then that matters. (01:17:15): But what ended up happening is we ended up looking at the data, and I can't take credit for this. My colleague at the time, Rob Andrews, had identified this. He was the head of growth marketing. He was a peer of mine that basically, this is 2016-ish days, the average person would come on Instagram and retain, but then leave after 7, 8, 9 months. We'd see a flattening in a retention curve, but then we would see it dip again, which was very weird. And we're like, why is this happening? And it turned out that what was happening anecdotally is that people were revving up Instagram, following a bunch of people, following a lot of celebrities, actually, because the celebrities were being shown, and then when they actually went to make their first post, a few months later-
turns.zh: 我认为，实际上有趣的一件事是，作为一个有趣的故事，但没有被太多谈论，我认为早期的 Instagram 是建立在……它的建立方式是每个关注者都是平等的。我的意思是，如果我关注了你，莱尼，或者如果我关注了金·卡戴珊，我关注了赛琳娜·戈麦斯，所有关注都被视为同等重要。这实际上是一个非常重要的事实。由于几个原因，这是一个非常重要的因素。第一，早期使用 Instagram 的名人显然从中受益，因为名人会比普通人先获得关注。这并不意味着他们的追随者没有意义。只是当你拥有一个针对点击和关注进行优化的机器学习时，那就很重要了。 (01:17:15)：但最终发生的事情是我们最终查看了数据，这不能归功于我。我当时的同事罗布·安德鲁斯（Rob Andrews）已经发现了这一点。他是增长营销的主管。他是我的一个同事，基本上，这是 2016 年左右的日子，一般人会在 Instagram 上停留并保留，但在 7、8、9 个月后离开。我们会看到保留曲线变平，但随后我们会看到它再次下降，这非常奇怪。我们想，为什么会发生这种情况？事实证明，有趣的是，人们正在加速 Instagram，关注一群人，关注很多名人，实际上，因为名人正在被展示，然后当他们真正去发布他们的第一个帖子时，几个月后 -

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: ... being shown. And then when they actually went to make their first post a few months later, none of their friends were following them. And so there was posting into an echo chamber and anecdotally people would stop using the product because they felt bad. We hypothesized that no one was liking or following or commenting on their posts. And so we had to do this thing. We called it the connections pivot, right in like 2016 ... Actually, 2017, where we had to convince Kevin and Mikey that it was actually not the right thing to do to prioritize celebrities to everybody because we were basically biting bite your nose to spank your face, whatever that is, because the regular person wasn't having a great experience. (01:18:44): And so it doesn't mean that we shouldn't recommend celebrities, but Jeff recommended celebrities to people who are already on there. They already have their graph. And the most important thing to do is actually get regular human-to-human connections in the first whatever, when people first sign up so that when you let me actually go make your first post, your friends would see it and you would be validated and you would feel like, okay, this is a police for me. I have a community here. (01:19:11): And so that connection pivot was critical. It changed ... Literally, angle-changed the retention on Instagram. And so if you about Instagram's growth, there was a TechCrunch article about Instagram's growth at I think 2017, 2018 when we were going 40, 50% year over year. And obviously, there was a lot that went into that skyrocket. People think that stories was the sole reason why we grew and story brought us a lot of people, but we literally, our attention doubled over the course of a year and a half. If you could imagine, imagine if your bank account, the interest rate doubles every month, you know what I mean? It was incredible. This shift in making sure that people got connected with their friends early on changed the way that people perceive the value. And so a lot of the top-of-funnel work that we did, a lot of the activation work that we did really paid off in spades ultimately.
turns.zh: ...正在展示。几个月后，当他们真正发布第一篇帖子时，他们的朋友都没有关注他们。因此，有人在回声室中发帖，据说人们会因为感觉不好而停止使用该产品。我们假设没有人喜欢、关注或评论他们的帖子。所以我们必须做这件事。我们称之为“联系枢纽”，就像 2016 年一样……实际上，在 2017 年，我们必须说服 Kevin 和 Mikey，让所有人优先考虑名人实际上并不是正确的做法，因为我们基本上是咬着鼻子打你的脸，不管是什么，因为普通人没有很好的体验。 (01:18:44)：所以这并不意味着我们不应该推荐名人，但杰夫向已经在那里的人推荐了名人。他们已经有了图表。最重要的是，当人们第一次注册时，首先要做的就是建立定期的人与人之间的联系，这样当你让我真正去发表你的第一篇帖子时，你的朋友会看到它，你会得到验证，你会觉得，好吧，这是我的警察。我这里有一个社区。 (01:19:11)：因此连接枢纽至关重要。它改变了......从字面上看，角度改变了 Instagram 上的保留率。因此，如果您了解 Instagram 的增长，TechCrunch 上有一篇文章介绍了 Instagram 在 2017 年和 2018 年的增长情况，当时我们的增长率为 40%、50%。显然，这种飙升涉及很多因素。人们认为故事是我们成长的唯一原因，故事给我们带来了很多人，但实际上，我们的注意力在一年半的时间里翻了一番。如果你能想象，想象一下如果你的银行账户利率每月翻一番，你明白我的意思吗？这太不可思议了。这种确保人们尽早与朋友建立联系的转变改变了人们感知价值的方式。因此，我们所做的很多漏斗顶部的工作，我们所做的很多激活工作最终确实得到了回报。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I'm curious, what's the most impactful thing you've shipped/led to in terms of impact and experiment launch?
turns.zh: 哇。我很好奇，就影响力和实验启动而言，您交付/促成的最有影响力的事情是什么？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: At Instagram, we saw this big problem where people were logging out and not being able to get back into their account. It was crazy. Hundreds of thousands of people a day could not get back into their account. It was because ... And when I say could not get back into the account, I mean they literally would try and 28 days later, we would never see them again. And we thought it was a problem because they didn't remember where their email was, which email they signed up with or what their actual handle was or what their password was. We were losing 10, 12 million people a year from what we called account access churn. So we worked on this problem and we had spent a lot of time in South Asia and Southeast Asia trying to understand how to grow the product. And from that time we realized that it's important actually for people to be able to log out. (01:21:14): We don't want to restrict people's ability to log out because there are many people in the world who don't want to use background data because they're on prepaid phone plans or they don't have a lot of money and they want to share their phone with a sibling and so they log out. And so it's really important. And so we don't want to take away that behavior, but we did have to do a better job of helping them get back in. (01:21:40): So we did two things. One was there used to be a time, and you can probably find it on Google if you did an archive search where if you wanted to log into your Instagram account, there would be a tab for your email and then there would be a tab for your handle. And we didn't really make it easy for you to log in with your phone number either. You had to get to the right tab and the right place to get the right thing. And so we did this omnibox experience where it was just like email, phone handle, put it all in one place and we made it super simple for you. And the second time, if you tried it twice and it didn't work, if we knew that you were on a trusted device, we would just send you a text message and say, Hey, are you trying to log in? That solved half the problem. (01:22:23): And then the other half, what we did, and this still exists today on Instagram. When you log out we say, Hey Lenny, it looks like you're going to log out, do you want us to save your credentials on your advice so you don't have to worry about your password? And then we later added an ability to have a password. And that's all basically the other half. (01:22:40): And so just being really thoughtful around what is actually the core job that people are trying to do because a bad experience would've been like, Hey, let's make it really hard for people to walk out. And then how do we ... One or two experiments really help people to get back into the experience. And so what was interesting was that we were able to solve this ... And this actually helped drive public 15, 20 million extra month active users a year, but what was also super interesting was that it helped us to realize that getting people back into their account more drove more account content creation on incident in ways that we didn't expect. And so because we were getting people back into the account, people getting into the second account and getting into the third account and they were going into their finsta account and creating content more. And so that actually led to the creation of a multiple accounts team, which is what has made it easy for you to navigate between accounts on Instagram today. (01:23:42): And so that was understandable actually coming to life. It was, Hey, we're going to do the understand work to figure out how to solve account access issues and we're going to solve it. And solving it, when we looked at the data, we're like, Hey, why is all this account, why is all this content creation happening? That was not what we were expecting and where is it happening? And it was happening from second and third accounts. And so that made us realize that oh, people were not only getting locked out of their first accounts, but they were actually creating a lot on the second and third accounts. How can we make it easy for them to get and navigate between their first account, whether it's your account and a business account or your account and [inaudible 01:24:19] account or a bakery account, you know what I mean? And so that created a multiple accounts team, which I ended up owning and that ended up even becoming a bigger effort after I left. (01:24:26): So that's an example of understand work, solve a real problem, real-solve and solving massive solution, massive impact, creating new data that you didn't expect that drives new understand work, which creates a whole new team to allow you to move around your Instagram account more seamlessly. And you can see this now when you go to post, you can decide, okay, I want to post as Lenny, I want to post as this other thing, or when I want to write a story, you can change anywhere. And that was all an effort that originally came out of this realization.
turns.zh: 在 Instagram，我们看到了一个大问题，即人们退出后无法返回他们的帐户。太疯狂了。每天有数十万人无法重新访问他们的帐户。这是因为……当我说无法回到帐户时，我的意思是他们确实会尝试，但 28 天后，我们再也见不到他们了。我们认为这是一个问题，因为他们不记得他们的电子邮件地址在哪里，他们注册的电子邮件地址是什么，或者他们的实际用户名是什么，或者他们的密码是什么。我们每年因所谓的帐户访问流失而失去 10、1200 万人。所以我们致力于解决这个问题，我们在南亚和东南亚花了很多时间试图了解如何种植该产品。从那时起，我们意识到人们能够注销实际上很重要。 (01:21:14)：我们不想限制人们注销的能力，因为世界上有很多人不想使用后台数据，因为他们使用预付费电话套餐，或者他们没有很多钱，并且想与兄弟姐妹共享手机，所以他们注销。所以这非常重要。因此，我们不想消除这种行为，但我们确实必须更好地帮助他们重新融入。(01:21:40)：所以我们做了两件事。一个是曾经有一段时间，如果你进行档案搜索，你可能可以在谷歌上找到它，如果你想登录你的 Instagram 帐户，会有一个用于你的电子邮件的选项卡，然后会有一个用于你的用户名的选项卡。我们也没有真正让您轻松使用电话号码登录。您必须进入正确的选项卡和正确的位置才能获得正确的东西。因此，我们做了这种多功能盒体验，就像电子邮件、电话手柄一样，将所有内容放在一个地方，我们让一切变得非常简单。第二次，如果您尝试了两次但没有成功，如果我们知道您使用的是受信任的设备，我们只会向您发送一条短信，并说：“嘿，您正在尝试登录吗？”这就解决了一半的问题。 (01:22:23)：然后是另一半，我们所做的，至今仍然存在于 Instagram 上。当您注销时，我们会说，嘿 Lenny，您似乎要注销，您是否希望我们根据您的建议保存您的凭据，以便您不必担心您的密码？然后我们后来添加了拥有密码的功能。这基本上就是另一半了。 (01:22:40)：因此，要认真思考人们正在尝试做的核心工作实际上是什么，因为糟糕的经历会像，嘿，让我们让人们很难走出去。然后我们如何……一两个实验真正帮助人们重新获得体验。有趣的是，我们能够解决这个问题……这实际上帮助每年增加了 15、2000 万的月度活跃用户，但同样非常有趣的是，它帮助我们认识到，让人们更多地回到他们的帐户，会以我们意想不到的方式推动更多的帐户内容创建。因为我们让人们重新进入帐户，人们进入第二个帐户并进入第三个帐户，他们进入他们的 finsta 帐户并创建更多内容。因此，这实际上导致了多帐户团队的创建，这使得您今天可以轻松地在 Instagram 帐户之间导航。 (01:23:42)：所以这是可以理解的。嘿，我们将做理解工作，找出如何解决帐户访问问题，我们将解决它。解决这个问题时，当我们查看数据时，我们会想，嘿，为什么会有这些帐户，为什么会发生所有这些内容创建？这不是我们所期待的，它发生在哪里？这是从第二个和第三个帐户发生的。这让我们意识到，哦，人们不仅被锁定在他们的第一个帐户之外，而且他们实际上在第二个和第三个帐户上创造了很多东西。我们如何才能让他们轻松获取并在他们的第一个帐户之间导航，无论是您的帐户和企业帐户还是您的帐户和 [听不清 01:24:19] 帐户或面包店帐户，您知道我的意思吗？因此，这就创建了一个多客户团队，我最终拥有了这个团队，在我离开后，这甚至成为了一项更大的工作。 (01:24:26)：这是一个理解工作、解决实际问题、真正解决和解决大规模解决方案、巨大影响、创建你意想不到的新数据的例子，这些数据会推动新的理解工作，从而创建一个全新的团队，让你可以更无缝地在你的 Instagram 帐户中移动。现在，当您发帖时，您可以看到这一点，您可以决定，好吧，我想以莱尼的身份发帖，我想以其他东西的身份发帖，或者当我想写一个故事时，您可以在任何地方进行更改。这一切都是出于这种认识而做出的努力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how many of these huge impact stories are just such straightforward, simple things like just let people log in more easily, help them log out more effectively, fine, show them their friends versus celebrities. So many of these stories are often just really simple ideas that lead to such profound change. The log-out example is interesting. At Airbnb, we found the log-out was actually causing a lot of churn also, but they went ... Initially, they went with a simple solution of just extend the session, log-out link instead of a week, make it two weeks or three weeks or four weeks. You pointed out with Instagram, people actually wanted to log out. They're like, let's leave that alone. Start with making it easier to log back in.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这些具有巨大影响力的故事中有很多都是如此简单明了的事情，比如让人们更轻松地登录，帮助他们更有效地注销，很好，向他们展示他们的朋友与名人。很多这样的故事往往只是非常简单的想法，但却导致了如此深刻的变化。注销的例子很有趣。在 Airbnb，我们发现注销实际上也造成了很多客户流失，但他们采取了……最初，他们采用了一个简单的解决方案，即延长会话、注销链接而不是一周，使其为两周、三周或四周。你指出，在 Instagram 上，人们实际上想退出。他们就像，让我们别管它。首先让重新登录变得更容易。

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 这是正确的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Man, you're so full of amazing stories. I'm curious with Facebook, maybe just as I wrap up here, is there anything there? Because you were an early growth PM at Facebook. You worked a lot on friends and helping people discover their friends. Is there anything in there that would be interesting to share?
turns.zh: 惊人的。伙计，你真是充满了精彩的故事。我对 Facebook 很好奇，也许就在我结束本文时，那里有什么东西吗？因为您是 Facebook 的早期增长产品经理。你在朋友方面做了很多工作，帮助人们发现他们的朋友。里面有什么有趣的东西可以分享吗？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: In my time, so I joined Instagram or Facebook in 2014 and I was responsible for people recommendations globally. And at the time, Facebook was at scale and big and dominated North America. And so really the focus area at the time was South Asia and Southeast Asia. And we noticed a lot of really interesting things, especially in India. Facebook seemed to be broken from a people graph perspective. The data was telling us people didn't have as many friends in common. In the US, it might've been on just making up a number. On average, we saw 22 friends in common when you make a friendship connection. But in India, it was like seven, right? And then there was a lot of friending and messaging or friending and unfriending. We're like, what's going on here? So we had some hypotheses from the data, we ran a bunch of tests. Nothing seemed to work and be a breakthrough. (01:26:44): So actually, at that time, I had to propose and they agreed to do this. We needed to do understand work. So we were literally on the ground in India every three months took a team of engineers with me. I'm talking like we're in Delhi in people's homes and Mumbai, and we went to go investigate what was going on, watch people make friends, watch them use people you may know and really understand what was happening and see what was going on because we felt like there was context that we were missing. (01:27:14): There was a lot of things that we learned. It was mind-blowing. But one of the most interesting things, Lenny, was that we watched people try to make friends and we said, "Hey wait, that's their profile page. Why aren't you looking at it?" And they would say, "Well, that doesn't have any relevant information for me, so I need to go look in the pictures." They're like, "Well, why doesn't the profile page have relevant information for you? That's where the information's supposed to be." And they're like, "Listen, this guy's named Amit Kumar. I have 10 friends named Amit Kumar. What is this page going to tell me?" And they would scroll down, they'd be like, "All of these fields are not relevant to me." And so you look at it, Facebook at the time, it was very Western-centric. It's probably still is, it was like name, it was like school you went to, job title, affiliations, that kind of stuff. That's all Western paradigms. Some of these people are like, my friends sell jeans at a market. None of this is relevant. You don't even know the name of the school. Sometimes it might be a number or something. And so all of the descriptors that we take for granted were not relevant and the names were very common. (01:28:24): This was really illuminating. So what they would do is go look at pictures and say, is this my friend's car or is this my friend's ... Can I see my friend's animal and what's available? And it was interesting because the understand work, at least the more realization. So we went back to Menlo Park with the data, turned out ... We said, okay, let's look at the data in a different way. What are the most common names on Facebook? And we looked at, and the top 10 common names are Indian names. And the most common name was Amit Kumar. And there was like 250,000 people a month who used Amit Kumar who were real people. So imagine you're in Bangalore and you're trying to find your buddy named Amit Kumar. It's probably 5,000 that we could possibly recommend. So super interesting was like the cultural context was so different. So we had to get creative, find creative ways to figure out how to solve it.
turns.zh: 在我那个时代，我在 2014 年加入了 Instagram 或 Facebook，负责全球范围内的人员推荐。当时，Facebook 规模庞大，在北美占据主导地位。因此，当时的重点区域实际上是南亚和东南亚。我们注意到很多非常有趣的事情，尤其是在印度。从人物图谱的角度来看，Facebook 似乎已经被打破了。数据告诉我们，人们没有那么多共同的朋友。在美国，这可能只是编造一个数字。平均而言，当您建立友谊关系时，我们会看到 22 个共同朋友。但在印度，这个数字大约是七个，对吧？然后有很多交友和消息，或者交友和取消交友。我们想，这里发生了什么事？因此，我们根据数据提出了一些假设，并进行了一系列测试。似乎没有什么能发挥作用，也没有什么突破。 (01:26:44)：所以实际上，当时我必须提出，他们同意这样做。我们需要做理解工作。因此，我们每三个月都会派出一支工程师团队前往印度实地考察。我说的就像我们在德里和孟买的人们家里一样，我们去调查正在发生的事情，观察人们交朋友，观察他们使用你可能认识的人，真正了解正在发生的事情，看看正在发生什么，因为我们觉得我们缺少了一些背景。 (01:27:14)：我们学到了很多东西。这真是令人兴奋。但最有趣的事情之一，莱尼，是我们看到人们试图交朋友，我们说，“嘿等等，那是他们的个人资料页面。你为什么不看看它呢？”他们会说：“好吧，这对我来说没有任何相关信息，所以我需要去看看照片。”他们会说，“好吧，为什么个人资料页面没有与你相关的信息？那才是信息应该在的地方。”他们会说，“听着，这个人叫 Amit Kumar。我有 10 个朋友叫 Amit Kumar。这个页面会告诉我什么？”他们会向下滚动，他们会说，“所有这些领域都与我无关。”所以你看，当时的 Facebook，它非常以西方为中心。可能仍然是，就像名字，就像你上过的学校，职位，隶属关系，诸如此类的东西。这就是西方的范式。其中一些人就像，我的朋友在市场上卖牛仔裤。这些都不相关。你甚至不知道学校的名字。有时它可能是一个数字或其他东西。因此，我们认为理所当然的所有描述符都是不相关的，并且名称非常常见。 (01:28:24)：这确实很有启发。所以他们会做的就是看照片并说，这是我朋友的车还是我朋友的……我可以看看我朋友的动物吗？有什么可用的？这很有趣，因为理解是有效的，至少是更多的实现。所以我们带着数据回到门洛帕克，结果......我们说，好吧，让我们以不同的方式来看看数据。 Facebook 上最常见的名字是什么？我们发现，前 10 个常见名字都是印度名字。最常见的名字是阿米特·库马尔。每月大约有 250,000 人使用 Amit Kumar，他们是真实的人。想象一下，您在班加罗尔，正在尝试寻找您的好友阿米特·库马尔 (Amit Kumar)。我们可能推荐的可能是 5,000。非常有趣的是，文化背景是如此不同。所以我们必须发挥创造力，找到创造性的方法来解决这个问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The power of understand work shines again. We have a recurring segment on this podcast called Fail Corner where ask guests to share a time they failed in their career and what they learned from that experience because a lot of people look at your career and your story and just like, holy shit, what a journey. I will never be able to achieve this. Is there a time when things didn't go well and something that you took away from that experience?
turns.zh: 理解工作的力量再次闪耀。我们在这个播客上有一个反复出现的部分，名为“失败角”，要求嘉宾分享他们在职业生涯中失败的经历以及他们从这次经历中学到的东西，因为很多人看着你的职业生涯和你的故事，就像，天啊，这真是一段旅程。我永远无法实现这一目标。是否有过事情进展不顺利的时候，你从那次经历中学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: Probably for me, I think my time at Instacart was probably not my best time. I think I went to Instacart with a vision of what I felt the product could be or should be. And it was I think a big story that I deeply believed, but I was not, I think aware or in tune with what the DNA of the company was at the time, which was it was like a company that was really great at operations because that was the core of what they did. And they were really building out a lot of their product experience and a lot of what the new function. And so I think what they needed at the time was a much more tactical in the weeds, get your hands dirty, do, do, do because they hadn't really seen that before. And what I wanted to deliver in that experience was more building the right systems, the right people, the right processes so that we can figure out how to institutionalize the work. (01:30:46): And I think for me that was probably my biggest oversight is that I think they needed more tactical and I was more ... I don't want to say in the clouds, but more thinking about where do we want to go with the experience that we need to build versus let me get deep in the funnel data. It felt like it became loggerheads where I didn't feel like I was probably either delivering what they wanted or being supported in the way that I wanted to be supported.
turns.zh: 可能对我来说，我认为我在 Instacart 的时光可能不是我最好的时光。我认为我进入 Instacart 时是带着对产品可能或应该是什么的愿景。我认为这是一个我深信不疑的大故事，但我认为当时我并没有意识到或不了解公司的 DNA，这就像一家非常擅长运营的公司，因为这是他们所做的核心。他们确实积累了大量的产品体验和新功能。所以我认为他们当时需要的是更具战术性的杂草，亲力亲为，做，做，做，因为他们以前从未真正见过这一点。我想通过这次经历更多地构建正确的系统、正确的人员、正确的流程，以便我们能够弄清楚如何将工作制度化。 (01:30:46)：我认为对我来说，这可能是我最大的疏忽，我认为他们需要更多的战术，而我更……我不想说在云端，而是更多地思考我们想要将我们需要构建的体验带到哪里，而不是让我深入了解漏斗数据。感觉就像是陷入了争执，我觉得我可能要么没有提供他们想要的东西，要么以我想要的方式得到支持。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is the lesson there to spend more time and understand work before you take a job to make sure you're aligned with what they're looking for?
turns.zh: 在你接受工作之前，是否应该花更多的时间来了解工作，以确保你符合他们的要求？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: That is actually the lesson. And I think it's part of that is it's doing that. One of my takeaways is do that not only with the people there but with the people who've left it to, but the people who've left the company will give you a perspective that is raw and different and much more I think aligned with what you want to hear. And it may or may not be the same, but I think the people ... This isn't specific to Instacart. Whenever you talk to people who are at the company, they're always try to tell you the best version of the company. The people who left will tell you what the worst version or their version and it's on you to triangulate that information, but you need both sides.
turns.zh: 这实际上就是教训。我认为这是其中的一部分，因为它正在这样做。我的收获之一是，不仅要与那里的人，还要与那些已经离开公司的人一起这样做，而且离开公司的人会给你一个原始的、不同的观点，而且我认为更符合你想听到的观点。它可能相同，也可能不同，但我认为人们……这并不是 Instacart 特有的。每当你与公司里的人交谈时，他们总是试图告诉你公司最好的一面。离开的人会告诉你最糟糕的版本或他们的版本是什么，你需要对这些信息进行三角测量，但你需要双方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Love that lesson. Bangaly, is there anything else that you want to share or leave listeners with before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 喜欢那节课。 Bangaly，在我们开始激动人心的闪电回合之前，您还有什么想与听众分享或留给听众的吗？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: No, I think we've got a lot.
turns.zh: 不，我想我们已经有很多了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We have. With that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got six questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 我们有。至此，我们进入了非常激动人心的闪电回合。我有六个问题要问你。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: I am ready to go.
turns.zh: 我准备走了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First question, what are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 第一个问题，您向其他人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: Few I've recommended most of them are Over My Shoulder, actually Range by David Epstein. I think are really critical PM work really being able to be a master of a lot of different things or somewhat deep in a lot of different things. Deep Work, Cal Newport, kind of clearing space to be focused and do the things thinking about the most important work in a deep and undisturbed way. And then Start At The End by Matt Waller, who's a behavioral scientist buddy of mine. Really thoughtful book, helps you really think about what you're building, but in a way that's more holistic.
turns.zh: 我很少推荐它们，大多数都是《Over My Shoulder》，实际上是大卫·爱泼斯坦的《Range》。我认为 PM 工作真的很重要，能够成为很多不同事物的大师，或者在很多不同的事物上有一定的深度。深度工作，加州纽波特，一种清理空间，让你能够集中精力，以一种深入且不受干扰的方式思考最重要的工作。然后是我的行为科学家好友马特·沃勒 (Matt Waller) 的《从结尾开始》(Start At The End)。一本真正有思想的书，可以帮助你真正思考你正在构建的东西，但以一种更全面的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite interview question that you like to ask candidates when you're interviewing them?
turns.zh: 在面试应聘者时，您有最喜欢问的面试问题吗？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: I've got a relatively new one that I love. This works exceptionally well I believe for more senior hires, whether they're like group product managers, directors, or even kind of senior ICs. I go through and I think about what are the four, usually five skills that are really critical for someone to have in this job. And I think about them myself and I think about the archetypes of what is the ratio I want of these? But then I ask them, I say, Hey, take out a piece of paper or take out your laptop. I'm going to give you five skills and I want you to stack-rank them for me. One to five. So one being the one you're strongest at and five being the one you're relatively weakest at. (01:33:41): So it's way better than saying give me your strengths and weaknesses. It also forces them to contextualize it against the skills that you're looking for, but it also helps you have a meaningful conversation around how they think about themselves and their self-awareness and to what extent they're ranking these skills based on the context they're in versus their own ability. (01:34:02): Sometimes you rank something a five because something you would just weak at because you haven't had to do because there's a strong function at that company. And so when they stack-rank it and then people are like ... I've asked this probably four or five times on a recent role. I hire people like, Ooh, this is really hard. But really good question. I usually will dig into what is number two and what's number four and number five, and why? And it really helps me to one, calibrate am I looking for the right person? And two, are their skills actually a match for what we need at this time?
turns.zh: 我有一件我很喜欢的相对较新的东西。我相信这对于更高级的员工来说非常有效，无论他们是集团产品经理、总监，甚至是高级 IC。我会仔细研究并思考对于从事这份工作的人来说真正至关重要的四种（通常是五种）技能是什么。我自己思考它们，思考我想要的比例是多少的原型？但后来我问他们，我说，嘿，拿出一张纸或拿出你的笔记本电脑。我将向您提供五项技能，并希望您为我对它们进行堆叠排名。一比五。因此，其中一项是您最擅长的一项，五项是您相对最弱的一项。 (01:33:41)：所以这比说告诉我你的优点和缺点要好得多。它还迫使他们将其与您正在寻找的技能结合起来，但它也可以帮助您围绕他们如何看待自己和自我意识进行有意义的对话，以及他们根据自己所处的环境与自己的能力对这些技能进行排名的程度。 (01:34:02)：有时你将某件事排在五分，因为某件事是你不擅长的，因为你不必这样做，因为该公司有强大的功能。因此，当他们对它进行堆叠排名时，人们就像……我在最近的一个角色中可能已经问过这个问题四五次了。我雇用这样的人，哦，这真的很难。但这确实是个好问题。我通常会深入研究什么是第二号，什么是第四号和第五号，为什么？它确实帮助我校准我是否在寻找合适的人？第二，他们的技能真的符合我们目前的需求吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love when I hear a question I've never heard before. That is genius. Next question, do you have a favorite product you've recently discovered that you really like?
turns.zh: 我喜欢听到以前从未听过的问题。那是天才。下一个问题，您最近发现有您真正喜欢的最喜欢的产品吗？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: I think one that I enjoy quite a lot ... Actually, it's really kind of ... It's really simple, but amazing is this app called Flighty. You heard of it? F-L-I-G-H-T-Y.
turns.zh: 我认为我非常喜欢这个应用程序...实际上，它真的有点...它非常简单，但令人惊奇的是这个名为 Flighty 的应用程序。你听说过吗？轻浮。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 不。

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: It is a travel app and it manages all of your flight itineraries and your friends' itineraries. But the reason why I love it is it goes two or three clicks deeper than the average travel app or your airline app and it tells you when your inbound plane is running late, it helps you to understand where the gates on. My wife was just in Madrid last week. And she texted me saying, "Hey, I'm at the airport but no gate is announced." I looked at Flighty, I'm like, "Your gate is E67. It's actually been assigned but it hasn't been announced." And this happens a lot in Europe. You'll be there and they won't tell you the gate until an hour beforehand. (01:35:28): So it gives you so much information right before. It's actually publicly announced, which is really helpful, especially if you really need to be somewhere because oftentimes I know if my plane's going to be late and if I need to rebook before anyone else does, which helps you, gives you a better chance of getting somewhere. Or I will be able to get to a gate, I get to SFO and it might not be on the board at SFO, but I know exactly where it gave you this. So really a great app. Can't say enough about it.
turns.zh: 它是一款旅行应用程序，可管理您的所有航班行程和您朋友的行程。但我喜欢它的原因是它比一般的旅行应用程序或航空公司应用程序更深入两到三次点击，它会告诉您进港飞机何时晚点，它可以帮助您了解登机口在哪里。我妻子上周刚在马德里。她给我发短信说：“嘿，我在机场，但没有宣布登机口。”我看着Flighty，我想，“你的登机口是E67。它实际上已经被分配了，但还没有宣布。”这种情况在欧洲经常发生。你会到达那里，直到提前一小时他们才会告诉你登机口。 (01:35:28)：所以它之前就给了你很多信息。它实际上是公开宣布的，这非常有帮助，特别是如果您确实需要去某个地方，因为我经常知道我的飞机是否会晚点，以及我是否需要在其他人之前重新预订，这对您有帮助，让您有更好的机会到达某个地方。或者我将能够到达登机口，我到达 SFO，它可能不在 SFO 的板上，但我确切地知道它在哪里给了你这个。所以这确实是一个很棒的应用程序。对此不能说太多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm downloading it right now. It's got a bazillion reviews, five stars. Thank you for the recommendation. Incredibly useful.
turns.zh: 我现在正在下载。它有无数的评论，五颗星。谢谢你的推荐。非常有用。

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: Of course.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm trying out a new question. You've joined a bunch of different companies. What's one thing that you've done in the first 90 days at the job that has made a big impact?
turns.zh: 我正在尝试一个新问题。你已经加入了很多不同的公司。在您上任的前 90 天里，您做过的对您产生重大影响的一件事是什么？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: I go and I sit in team meetings and see how they operate. I just listen. I talk to not only the PMs but the content designer and everyone, and I try to get to know them by both name and story. And what I mean by that, it's like oftentimes people, execs come in and they're like, what are we doing? What are we prioritizing? Why does it matter? And they don't really take the time to actually learn who the people are, what the story is, what they care about, what they're passionate about, both professionally and personally and really try to understand how the team is working from that person's perspective. (01:36:52): And what I find is actually when I do that, people are way more willing to hear ... When it is time for me to share my thoughts, they're way more invested because they believe I'm invested in that.
turns.zh: 我去参加团队会议，看看他们是如何运作的。我只是听着。我不仅与产品经理交谈，还与内容设计师和每个人交谈，我尝试通过名字和故事来了解他们。我的意思是，人们、高管经常进来，他们会问，我们在做什么？我们优先考虑什么？为什么这很重要？他们并没有真正花时间去真正了解这些人是谁，有什么故事，他们关心什么，他们热衷于什么，无论是专业还是个人，也没有真正尝试从那个人的角度理解团队是如何工作的。 (01:36:52)：我发现实际上当我这样做时，人们更愿意听到......当我需要分享我的想法时，他们会更加投入，因为他们相信我对此进行了投入。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Two more questions. Do you have a favorite life motto that you really like and find useful and often share with friends or family in work or in life?
turns.zh: 我喜欢那个。还有两个问题。您是否有一条您真正喜欢并且觉得有用并且经常在工作或生活中与朋友或家人分享的最喜欢的人生格言？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: I'm not big on mottos. There's one that I've actually been repeating. I don't remember. I got it done ... It might have been like Adam Grant or someone on Instagram, but it was ... It's one, I said it to a colleague of mine, he's like, "Wow, that really hit differently." I think it goes something like this. People and teams don't really reach ... They don't actually reach their goals. They fall to the level of their systems. (01:37:43): And that to me was really powerful because I struggle a lot with just being balanced in life, working out the way I want to and getting the right rest and making sure that I'm spending time in all the right places. And that's really like ... It's a goal of mine. But the problem is that I don't ... My system for that specifically, I tend to ... I'm not rigorous with it is when I need to be. (01:38:06): But on the other hand, at work, I'm very rigorous in the systems and processes. So really that saying to me really hits because it is both applicable to your life and how you want to live your life but also how you want to run your teams.
turns.zh: 我不太热衷于座右铭。有一个我实际上一直在重复的。我不记得了。我完成了......这可能就像 Adam Grant 或 Instagram 上的某个人一样，但它是......这是一个，我对我的一位同事说，他就像，“哇，这真的很不同。”我认为事情是这样的。人们和团队并没有真正达到……他们实际上并没有达到他们的目标。他们下降到他们的系统的水平。 (01:37:43)：这对我来说真的很强大，因为我在生活中保持平衡、按照自己想要的方式锻炼、得到正确的休息以及确保我把时间花在所有正确的地方方面付出了很多努力。这真的就像......这是我的目标。但问题是我不……我的系统特别是，我倾向于……当我需要的时候，我对此并不严格。 (01:38:06): 但另一方面，在工作中，我对制度和流程非常严格。所以这句话对我来说确实很重要，因为它既适用于你的生活，也适用于你想要如何过自己的生活，也适用于你想要如何管理你的团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question. You mentioned that you were a dean at a school, a boarding school. Is there something that you take away from that experience that's going to sticks with you? I know you mentioned one thing about treat PM's skills are similar to teacher skills. There anything else there?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。你提到你是一所寄宿学校的院长。你从这次经历中学到的东西有没有让你难以忘怀的？我知道你提到过一件事，即对待 PM 的技能与老师的技能相似。那里还有别的事吗？

turns.speaker: Bangaly Kaba
turns.en: Actually, so I was a dean of a boarding school in Switzerland, which was actually one of the most fun and interesting times of my life. It was an American school in Switzerland just outside of Lugano, Switzerland, the Italian-speaking section. I learned a lot about myself during the time. I learned a lot about just relationships and people. I actually had a call with one of my old students this morning. She's like in her thirties now. This was like 20 years ago. So I still keep in touch with them. And I think that's the comment I made about knowing people by name and story matters a lot. It says a lot that 20 years later I'm still talking to some of these students who are their own adults running their own businesses. But also I think the human challenges and human connection, human problems, very universal. (01:39:24): This was a really interesting place when you had kids coming from a variety of different walks of life, some who lived in Azerbaijan or Kosovo and felt like ... The families felt like they couldn't be safe there, so they wanted to send the kids somewhere else.
